problems.title: [Iodine in brown algae]
problems.problem:
Problem 1. [Iodine in brown algae]

A weighed amount of brown algae (100 g) was extracted with water and the resulting solution irradiated with UV light in a closed reactor without removing oxygen until the complete transition of iodides into elemental iodine.

1. Write the reaction of iodine formation from inorganic iodide.

Note that the precipitate of iodine in the resulting solution did not form. After cetyltrimethylammonium bromide $\ce{C16H33(CH3)3NBr}$ (CTMA) was introduced into the solution, a salt $\mathbf{A}$ containing the organic cation precipitated. The precipitate was washed, dried and weighed; its weight was 1.205 g. The precipitate was dissolved in the mixture of ethanol – water (1:1 vol.) in a volumetric flask of 100 mL capacity and adjusted to the mark; then a 10.00-mL aliquot was taken and titrated with a 0.1000 M sodium thiosulfate solution until the color disappeared, which required 3.9 mL of the titrant.

2. What is the amount of iodine contained in precipitate $\mathbf{A}$? Record the probable composition of $\mathbf{A}$ and the reaction of its precipitation.

3. Calculate the iodine content in algae in g/100 g.

A weighed portion of NaI (8.0 mmol) was added to 100 mL of a 0.040 M solution of sodium iodate in 1 M HBr; as a result, after brief coloring, a nearly colorless solution of compound $\mathbf{B}$ was formed.

4. Write the reaction equation, if none of the substances was in excess. Note that the further addition of 12 mmol of solid NaI to the solution and an excess of CTMA yielded 12 mmol of precipitate $\mathbf{A}$.

5. Write the reaction of transformation of $\mathbf{B}$ into $\mathbf{A}$.

6. Write down the reaction of hydrolysis of $\mathbf{B}$. What medium (acidic or alkaline) will promote hydrolysis? Confirm with a reaction equation.

problems.title: [Fruit ripening regulators]
problems.problem:
Problem 2. [Fruit ripening regulators]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2016-1-2-fig1.png

Figure. Bananas treated with compound $\mathbf{B}$ at concentration varied from 0 to 0.005 ppm followed by treatment with compound $\mathbf{A}$ (300 ppm) and keeping under air for 7 days.

Two binary gaseous (under normal conditions) compounds $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ (containing 14.37% and 11.18% of element $\mathbf{X}$, respectively), regulate ripening of fruit and widely used during the transportation and storage of fruit and vegetables. Compound $\mathbf{A}$ is synthesized in the Nature by Yang cycle fragment of which is given in the following Scheme:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2016-1-2-fig2.png

Compound $\mathbf{B}$ is unnatural. Initially, it was synthesized by the treatment of methallyl chloride with a strong base. The side-product of this reaction is the compound $\mathbf{B'}$ which is more symmetrical than $\mathbf{B}$. However, this method is not practical as the dosage of gaseous compound $\mathbf{B}$ cannot be taken easily. In 2012, this problem was solved by chemists from Erum Biotechnologies (South Korea). They proposed method given in Scheme 2. The possibility of the dosage of $\mathbf{B}$ is based in this method on the fact that compound $\mathbf{E}$ under treatment with the calculated quantity of fluoride ion produces quantitatively the required amount of compound $\mathbf{B}$. $\mathbf{E}$ is obtained by mesylation of $\mathbf{D}$ which is the product of Kulinkovich reaction.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2016-1-2-fig3.png

1. Write down structural formulae of compounds $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{B'}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ accounting for fact that $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{B'}$ have the same carbon skeleton as that of the achiral compound $\mathbf{C}$.

2. Decipher structures $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{E}$ if it is known that these compounds are trans-isomers.

3. Calculate the required quantity (in mL) of 2.3 M solution of $\ce{Bu4NF}$ in DMF as well as minimum amount of $\mathbf{E}$ (in g) to obtain the concentration of $\mathbf{B}$ at 0.005 ppm level in the container with size of $12.0\cdot2.3\cdot2.4\,\mathrm{m}$.

problems.title: [Metal A from polymetallic sulfide ores and its oxidants]
problems.problem:
Problem 3. [Metal A from polymetallic sulfide ores and its oxidants]

The metal $\mathbf{A}$ obtained by coal reducing of its oxide $\mathbf{B}$ after sulfide burning. This sulfide is produced by processing polymetal (CuS, PbS) sulfide ores. Metal $\mathbf{A}$ is known as one of the major components of Wood's metal.

$\mathbf{A}$ is dissolved only in oxidizing acids. For example, reaction with 30% $\ce{HNO3}$ leads to nitrate $\mathbf{C}$, which is easily hydrolysed in water forming the basic salts, one of which composition can be written as $[\mathrm{A}_6\mathrm{O}_4(\mathrm{OH})_4](\mathrm{NO}_3)_6\cdot4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}$. Therefore, metal salts of $\mathbf{A}$ are dissolved in solution of the corresponding acids.

Addition of alkali to $\mathbf{C}$ leads to the precipitation of hydroxide $\mathbf{D}$. The compound $\mathbf{E}$ is produced by oxidation of $\mathbf{D}$ by potassium persulfate in alkaline medium. $\mathbf{E}$ is used in the practice of inorganic synthesis as a strong oxidant. Thus, the reaction of $\mathbf{E}$ with a transition metal sulfate affords another colored oxidant $\mathbf{F}$, which solution has an intense broad absorption band in the green region (550 nm).

$\mathbf{B}$ is formed when $\mathbf{D}$ is heated to $150\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, (the weight loss in this process is 10.4%). Compound $\mathbf{B}$ is a yellow crystals, it is usually prepared by thermolysis of various metal organic compounds of $\mathbf{A}$: acetates, β-diketonates and other MOCs. Sodium analogue of $\mathbf{E}$ is synthesized by fusion of $\mathbf{B}$ with sodium peroxide in an oxygen atmosphere.

1. Identify compounds $\mathbf{A}$ – $\mathbf{F}$ and write the mentioned reactions of their obtaining.

2. Specify the elemental composition of the Wood's metal, and select faithful answers of the Wood's metal usage from proposed in the answer sheet.

3. Draw six-core structure of the cation $[\mathrm{A}_6\mathrm{O}_4(\mathrm{OH})_4]^{6+}$, if it is known that the structure contains such elements of symmetry as three two-fold axes and three mirror planes.

4. What is the color of the compound $\mathbf{F}$? According what model (VBT, CFT, MOT) can be the appearance of $\mathbf{F}$'s color explained?

The problem of obtaining $\mathbf{B}$ has acquired a special significance in recent decades, since HTSC properties of complex oxide materials containing $\mathbf{A}$ have been discovered.

5. Specify features of the superconducting state among the options listed in the answer sheet.

[The options for questions 2 and 5 are printed only in the answer sheet, which is not available.]

problems.title: [PlantBottle: plastic bottles from sugar-cane]
problems.problem:
Problem 4. [PlantBottle: plastic bottles from sugar-cane]

Aimed at minimizing the environmental impact, The Coca-Cola Company has developed and implemented production of the plastic bottles, which (as reported by the manufacturer) contain up to 30% of phytogenous materials. In reality, such bottles are molded of a single polymer $\mathbf{X}$, a product of ethylene glycol condensation with diprotic aromatic carboxylic acid $\ce{C8H6O4}$.

1. Suggest three isomeric structures of $\mathbf{X}$ and choose the one that is most likely used in the industrial production.

2. Based on the content of the phytogenous materials in the plastic packing (without the label and cap), determine what component of the plastics is produced from biological raw material.

Sugar-cane is predominantly used as a raw material for the production of biobottles, since it is among the plants, which most actively absorb atmospheric $\ce{CO2}$ and efficiently utilize photosynthesis.

3. Suggest the industrial method of production of the demanded component of the plastics from sugar-cane. Write down the corresponding reactions.

4. Is it possible to distinguish between the biobottle and the conventional plastic bottle, provided the geometry, size, surface morphology, etc. of the bottles are identical?

In a science educational review, the content of the biocomponent in the plastics produced by The Coca-Cola Company was calculated using two different approaches. The reported values were of 20% and 31.25%.

5. Demonstrate the ways of calculation leading to the reported results. For each variant, write down the corresponding math and/or chemical equations and formulae.

The PlantBottle technology was launched in 2009. 20 billion biobottles have been produced by the beginning of 2014. The Coca-Cola Company reported that this allowed saving 445000 barrels of oil (1 barrel = 159 L).

6. Estimate the mass of the bottle used in the calculations done by the Coca-Cola Company Marketing Department to demonstrate the ecological effect of the novel packing.

problems.title: [A synthesis from oxalic acid and permanganate in the dark]
problems.problem:
Problem 5. [A synthesis from oxalic acid and permanganate in the dark]

The procedure for the synthesis of the substance $\mathbf{A}$ is described below.

In the first stage, a 31.5 g of oxalic acid dihydrate is dissolved in 200 mL of water at 70–$75\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Then a 6.32 g of finely pounded potassium permanganate is added to the solution in small increments while stirring. After the reaction, 6.90 g of potassium carbonate was added slowly, and the resulting solution was cooled to 4–$5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and diluted with 160 mL of chilled water.

1. Write down the chemical equation occurring in the first stage of synthesis of $\mathbf{A}$.

The second stage of synthesis should, if possible, be carried out in complete darkness. 1.58 g of potassium permanganate ground into a fine powder is added to the solution obtained in the first stage of the synthesis. The mixture is then vigorously stirred for 10 min at 0–$2\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The resulting red-violet solution is cooled and filtered cold, then 200 mL of strongly chilled ethanol is added to it. The solution is left to crystallize in a mixture of ice and salt for 2 hours. The crystalline precipitate (potassium mass fraction is 23.92%) is separated on a sintered glass filter and dried at the room temperature in the air.

2. Determine the chemical formula of $\mathbf{A}$ and write down the equation that occurs in the second stage of the synthesis.

3. Write down the total equation of $\mathbf{A}$ synthesis described above and calculate its actual yield if the mass of the resulting product was 12.8 g.

If recovery of $\mathbf{A}$ is carried out in the light, it is contaminated by the substances $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ (mass fraction of potassium 22.65%).

4. Write down chemical formulas of $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ and the chemical equation of their formation.

Concentrated aqueous solutions of $\mathbf{A}$ has deep red-violet color. When diluted or acidified, the solution color changes to yellow-brown.

5. What causes the color change upon dilution or acidification of the aqueous solution of $\mathbf{A}$? Write down the chemical reaction.

problems.title: [Hydrogen atom: from the Rydberg formula to the Bohr model]
problems.problem:
Problem 6. [Hydrogen atom: from the Rydberg formula to the Bohr model]

In 1888 Rydberg and Ritz discovered an empirical formula which determines the positions of spectral lines of hydrogen atoms by light absorption:

$$\frac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right),$$

where $\lambda$ – wavelength, $R$ – Rydberg constant, $n_1$ and $n_2$ – natural numbers. A given spectral series corresponds to transfer (jump) of electron from different states $n_2$ to a given state $n_1$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \text{Spectral series} & n_1 & n_2 & \lambda,\ \mathrm{nm} \\ \hline \text{Layman} & 1 & 3 & \sim100 \\ \text{Layman} & 1 & & 121 \\ \hline \text{Brackket} & 4 & & 1456 \\ \hline \text{Ballmer} & & 3 & \end{array}$$

1. Using the data from the table, calculate the Rydberg constant $R$ and complete this table with the absent data.

In 1913 Bohr developed his model of Hydrogen atom. This model is based on the supposition that the atom has stationary circular orbits where electron is located without emission of energy. Electron transfer from orbit $n_1$ to $n_2$ is accompanied by absorption or emission of light (photon) with specific wavelength.

The potential energy of electron in the electrostatic field of the nuclei is

$$E_\mathrm{p} = -\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r_n},$$

where $e = 1.6\cdot10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$ – elementary charge, $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\cdot10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F/m}$ – electric constant, $r_n$ – radius of $n^\text{th}$ orbit. And $r_n = a_0 n^2$, $a_0$ – radius of $1^\text{st}$ Bohr orbit (Bohr's radius).

It is known that the value of kinetic energy of electron in Hydrogen atom is twice smaller than those of potential energy and it is opposite in sign.

2. Which series does correspond to transfer of electron to the ground state?

3. Knowing constant $R$, calculate the energy of 1 mole of hydrogen atoms in the ground state.

4. Calculate the Bohr's radius $a_0$ and minimal distance between $3^\text{rd}$ and $2^\text{nd}$ orbits.

5. Find the ionization energy of hydrogen atom.

6. Taking into account that the total energy of $\ce{H2}$ molecule is $-3070\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$ (energy is measured from the energy of nuclei and electrons at rest, situated at infinite distance from each other), calculate the bond energy between H atoms in this molecule.

Additional data: $h = 6.627\cdot10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\cdot s}$, $c = 3\cdot10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\cdot s^{-1}}$.

problems.title: [The bombardier beetle]
problems.problem:
Problem 7. [The bombardier beetle]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2016-1-7-fig1.png

The bombardier beetles are known for the unique defense mechanism. In case of danger they excrete a hot stream of the repellent solution frightening away the aggressor (see the figure). The stream is formed via the chemical reaction involving a pair of compounds fed into the reaction chamber from the reservoirs in the beetle body. One of the reactants is a representative of the hydroquinones class ($\mathbf{B}\mathrm{H}_2$).

1. Mass fraction of oxygen in $\mathbf{B}\mathrm{H}_2$ is of 25.78%. Determine the compound structure.

Hydrogen peroxide is the second component of the reaction mixture. The following set of the reaction occurs in the reaction chamber in the presence of catalase and peroxidase enzymes:

$$\mathbf{B}\mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{l}) \rightarrow \mathbf{B}(\mathrm{l}) + \ce{H2}(\mathrm{g})\ \ (1);\quad \ce{H2O2}(\mathrm{l}) \rightarrow \ce{H2O}(\mathrm{l}) + \tfrac{1}{2}\ce{O2}(\mathrm{g})\ \ (2);\quad \ce{H2}(\mathrm{g}) + \tfrac{1}{2}\ce{O2}(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow \ce{H2O}(\mathrm{l})\ \ (3).$$

2. Write down the resultant thermochemical equation of the reaction between $\mathbf{B}\mathrm{H}_2$ and $\ce{H2O2}$.

Standard enthalpies of formation of $\ce{H2O}$(l) and $\ce{H2O2}$(l) are of, $-285.83\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$ and $-187.78\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$, respectively.

3. Determine standard enthalpy of reactions (2) and (3).

Standard potential of the ($\mathbf{B}\mathrm{H}_2/\mathbf{B}$) electrode relative to the standard hydrogen electrode is of 0.7175 V at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and of 0.6805 V at $50\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

4. Determine standard enthalpy of reaction (1) and of the resultant reaction that you have reported in question 2.

The composition of the mixture in the reaction chamber of the beetle is as follows: 10 wt.% $\mathbf{B}\mathrm{H}_2$, 25 wt.% $\ce{H2O2}$, and water.

5. Assuming that the thermophysical properties of the mentioned reaction components are approximately the same as for water (specific heat capacity $4.2\,\mathrm{J/deg\cdot g}$ in the liquid phase and of $2\,\mathrm{J/deg\cdot g}$ in vapor phase, specific heat of evaporation $2256\,\mathrm{J/g}$), determine the final temperature of the excreted stream. Choose the proper type of the excreted mixture from the list in the Answers sheet.

[The list of mixture types for question 5 is printed only in the answer sheet, which is not available.]

problems.title: [Jenneskens' unusual hydrocarbon I]
problems.problem:
Problem 8. [Jenneskens' unusual hydrocarbon I]

In 1984, L. W. Jenneskens and co-workers synthesized for the first time hydrocarbon $\mathbf{I}$ with very unusual structure. The starting compound in their synthesis was a monocyclic hydrocarbon $\mathbf{X}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2016-1-8-fig1.png

This is known that: a) compound $\mathbf{A}$ and its isomer $\mathbf{B}$ can be described as products of 1,2- and 1,4-addition of dichlorocarbene to $\mathbf{X}$; b) $\mathbf{X}$ reacts with acrolein ($\ce{CH2=CH-CHO}$) affording bicyclic product $\mathbf{E}$; c) ozonation of 1 mol of $\mathbf{X}$ followed by ozonide reduction with zinc in acetic acid produces 2 mol of $\ce{CH2O}$ and 1 mol of $\mathbf{F}$, $^1$H NMR spectrum of which contains 3 signals with the relative intensities of 2:2:1; d) compound $\mathbf{D}$ has 4 diastereomers.

1. Write down structural formulae of $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{A}$ – $\mathbf{F}$.

2. Write down structures of diastereomers of $\mathbf{D}$.

Hydrocarbon $\mathbf{I}$ demonstrates chemical behavior different from that for the most arenes. Thus, it form addition products in reactions with electrophiles; in the presence of acid $\mathbf{I}$ isomerizes into thermodynamically more stable compound $\mathbf{II}$. The last reaction proceeds via the intermediate formation of isomeric carbocations $[\mathbf{III}]^+$ and $[\mathbf{IV}]^+$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2016-1-8-fig2.png

3. Write down structural formulae of compounds $\mathbf{II}$ – $\mathbf{IV}$, accounting for fact that $\mathbf{I}$ and $\mathbf{II}$ are positional isomers.

problems.title: [Conductometric titrations]
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (Analytical Chemistry section, problem 1). [Conductometric titrations]

Conductometry is the one of the oldest electrochemical methods of analysis. It is based on the measurement of conductivity $\sigma$ [S/m]. Conductivity is related to the existence of ions in solution. Each ion is characterized by the molar conductivity $\lambda$ [$\mathrm{S\cdot m^2/mol}$], which depends on its charge $z$ and mobility $\mu$ [$\mathrm{S\cdot m^2/C}$]: $\lambda = |z|\cdot\mu\cdot F$, where $F$ is Faraday constant. The total conductivity is the sum of the conductivities of each ion: $\sigma = \sum\sigma_\mathrm{i} = \sum\lambda_\mathrm{i}\cdot c_\mathrm{i}$ where $c_i$ is the concentration of the ion [$\mathrm{mol/m^3}$].

1. The mobilities of $\ce{OH-}$ and $\ce{H+}$ are $2.07\cdot10^{-7}$ and $3.63\cdot10^{-7}\,\mathrm{S\cdot m^2/C}$, respectively. Calculate the molar conductivities $\lambda(\ce{OH-})$, $\lambda(\ce{H+})$ and the conductivity ($\sigma$) of pure water.

In the first experiment, 50.0 mL of strong acid $\mathbf{HA}$ was titrated by a 0.500M solution of alkali. The graph represents the conductivity as function of the volume of the alkali solution (see Figure).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2016-2-1-fig1.png

2. Which ions contribute to the conductivity before equivalence point, in the equivalence point and after the equivalence point? Consider the water dissociation as negligible.

3. Determine the acid $\mathbf{HA}$ (HCl, $\ce{HClO4}$ or HBr) and alkali (LiOH, KOH or NaOH), taking into account that the molar conductivities of ions [$\mathrm{mS\cdot m^2/mol}$] are as follows:

$$\lambda(\ce{K+}) = 7.35,\ \lambda(\ce{Na+}) = 5.01,\ \lambda(\ce{Li+}) = 3.86,\ \lambda(\ce{Cl-}) = 7.63,\ \lambda(\ce{Br-}) = 7.80.\ \lambda(\ce{ClO4-}) = 6.52.$$

4. Calculate the solution conductivity after addition of 6.0 mL of the alkali solution.

In the second experiment, 20 mL of a mixture of HCl with a weak organic acid $\mathbf{H_nB}$ ($K_\mathrm{a}\sim10^{-5}$) was diluted to 100 mL and titrated by a 0.600M KOH solution. The results of titration are given in the table:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c} V,\ \mathrm{mL} & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 & 8 & \mathbf{10} & \mathbf{12} \\ \hline \sigma,\ \mathrm{S/m} & 0.600 & 0.489 & 0.377 & 0.267 & 0.233 & 0.278 & 0.324 & 0.489 & 0.655 & 0.985 & 1.312 \end{array}$$

5. How many protons of the weak acid $\mathbf{H_nB}$ have been titrated?

6. Calculate the concentration of both acids in the non-diluted (initial) solution.

problems.title: [Cobalt as potassium hexanitritocobaltate(III): titration errors]
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (Analytical Chemistry section, problem 2). [Cobalt as potassium hexanitritocobaltate(III): titration errors]

For the determination of the concentration of $\ce{CoCl2}$, a young man added 5.0 mL of 0.2M solution of potassium nitrite to 100 mL of the analyte aqueous solution, then he added 2 mL of acetate buffer, heated the solution to boiling and left it for 4 h. The obtained yellow precipitate of potassium hexanitritocobaltate(III) $\ce{K3[Co(NO2)6]}$ was filtered through a glass filter, washed on the filter with 0.01M solution of $\ce{KNO3}$, dissolved in sulfuric acid and transferred into a 100-mL volumetric flask. A 10.0-mL aliquot of that solution was titrated with a 0.0500M solution of potassium permanganate (until the purple color appeared). The titrant volume spent for that titration was 13.75 mL.

1. Give equations for the following reactions: a) formation of $\ce{K3[Co(NO2)6]}$; b) interaction of potassium permanganate with nitrite ion in acidic medium; c) interaction of potassium permanganate with $\ce{K3[Co(NO2)6]}$, if cobalt is completely converted into oxidation state +2.

2. Calculate the concentration of cobalt salt in the analyte solution according to titration results.

3. What factors affect the solubility of $\ce{K3[Co(NO2)6]}$ in the mother solution after precipitate formation? Choose the right answers: a) stability constant of complex ion $\ce{[Co(NO2)6]^{3-}}$; b) solubility product of the precipitate; c) concentration of $\ce{K+}$; d) concentration of Co(II); e) concentration of $\ce{NO2-}$.

4. Calculate the solubility of potassium hexanitritocobaltate(III) in the mother solution (g/L) if its solubility product is equal to $K_\mathrm{S} = [\ce{K+}]^3[\ce{Co(NO2)6^{3-}}] = 4.3\times10^{-10}$ and the stability constant of the complex ion is high enough.

5. Estimate the titration error (%) due to the solubility of precipitate in the mother solution (disregard the losses as a consequence of precipitate washing).

6. Determine the optimal volume of washing solution (0.01M $\ce{KNO3}$) corresponding to the minimal titration error if the latter is caused (1) by appearance of nitrite ions in the titration flask as a result of insufficient washing of the precipitate, and (2) by losses through precipitate washing due to its solubility in the washing solution. Draw the graphs for the both components of error as functions of washing solution volume $V_\mathrm{y}$. Assume that unwashed precipitate captures the mother solution in the amount equal to a half of its mass $m$. Take into account that each milliliter of the washing solution removes 1% of the captured mother solution volume.

problems.title: [Polarography]
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (Analytical Chemistry section, problem 3). [Polarography]

Polarography is a technique applied for the determination of metal ions. The potential between a dropping mercury cathode and a mercury pool anode is varied (for example, from 0.0 to –1.5 V), and the corresponding changes in current $I$ are measured. When reducible substances are present in the solution, a sharp rise in current occurs at the certain potential. The recorded plot of current against applied voltage $I = f(E)$ (polarogram) is characterized by wave height $h$ (cm), or diffusion current $I_\mathrm{max}$ (A), that are proportional to the concentration of the unknown ion, and by the potential at the midpoint of the wave $E_{1/2}$ (half-wave potential) depending on the nature of the analyte.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2016-2-3-fig1.png

Scheme of an apparatus for polarographic analysis: 1 – electrochemical cell (with pool mercury electrode); 2 – dropping mercury electrode; 3 – galvanometer; 4 – potentiometer; 5 – current source.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2016-2-3-fig2.png

1. A weighed amount of $\ce{PbCl2}$ was dissolved in 100 mL ($V_0$) of 1M $\ce{KNO3}$ solution (the salt is used to ensure conductivity). A 10.00-mL aliquote ($V_1$) of the prepared solution was transferred into the electrochemical cell and subjected to polarographic analysis. The polarographic wave obtained displays a height of 5.0 mm ($h_1$). After addition of 4.50 mL ($V_2$) of $\ce{PbCl2}$ solution ($c_2$ = 3 mg/L) into the cell the wave height became 8.1 mm ($h_2$). Derive the formulae and calculate the mass of $\ce{PbCl2}$ taken for the analysis.

2. Calculate the solubility product ($K_\mathrm{S}$) of $\ce{PbCl2}$, if the polarographic wave recorded during analysis of its saturated solution in 1M $\ce{KNO3}$ exhibits $I_\mathrm{max} = 43.2\,\mathrm{\mu A}$. If a standard $\ce{PbCl2}$ solution (5.0 mM) is analyzed under the same conditions, $I_\mathrm{max} = 13.6\,\mathrm{\mu A}$.

$$\begin{array}{l|l} \text{Ion} & E_{1/2},\ \mathrm{V} \\ \hline \text{Zn(II)} & -0.99 \\ \text{Cd(II)} & -0.62 \\ \text{Pb(II)} & -0.41 \\ \ce{O2} & -0.1,\ -0.9 \end{array}$$

3. A weighed sample of alloy containing zinc, lead and cadmium was dissolved and the polarogram of this solution was recorded (the potential was varied from 0 to –1.2V). Before the measurement an inert gas was passed through the solution in the cell.

a) Draw the current–potential plot on the graph (curve No 1), using the data from the table and the marked values of $I_\mathrm{max}$. Point out the proper $E_{1/2}$ values on each wave.

b) Draw the polarogram of this solution recorded without preliminary oxygen removal (curve No 2). Give the chemical equations for the half-reactions with oxygen that take place on the dropping mercury cathode in basic and acidic media.

[The graph with the marked values of $I_\mathrm{max}$ for question 3 is printed only in the answer sheet, which is not available.]

4. The potential corresponding to the reduction of complex $\mathrm{MetL_x}$ is described with equations: $E = E_{1/2}(\mathrm{Met}^{n+}) + 0.059/n\cdot\lg[\mathrm{Met}^{n+}] = E_{1/2}(\mathrm{MetL_x}) + 0.059/n\cdot\lg[\mathrm{MetL_x}]$, where $E_{1/2}(\mathrm{Met}^{n+})$ and $E_{1/2}(\mathrm{MetL_x})$ are the half-wave potentials for the free and complexed metal-ions, respectively; $[\mathrm{MetL_x}]$ and $[\mathrm{Met}^{n+}]$ are the concentrations in the equilibrium, and $n$ is the metal ion charge.

a) Give the reaction for the complex formation between lead(II) and glycine and the expression of the cumulative stability constant $\beta_2$ for the complex $\mathrm{Pb(gly)_2}$. What reactions involving glycine or lead(II) may compete with the complex formation in the neutral water solution? Give at least one reaction for the metal ion and one for the ligand.

b) Derive an equation for the calculation of half-wave potential for complex $\mathrm{Pb(gly)_2}$ reduction (use stability constant $\beta_2$). Calculate $E_{1/2}$ for ($\mathrm{Pb(gly)_2}$) in 0.5M glycine solution under pH ≈ 7–8, if $\beta_2 = 3.2\cdot10^{7}$. Compare the obtained value $E_{1/2}$ with that given in the table for $\ce{Pb^{2+}}$ ion. What is easier to reduce: complex $\mathrm{Pb(gly)_2}$ or aqueous ion $\ce{Pb^{2+}}$?

problems.title: [Classical and nonclassical tautomers of Luo and Crabtree]
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (Inorganic Chemistry section, problem 1). [Classical and nonclassical tautomers of Luo and Crabtree]

For the investigation of equilibrium between classical ($\mathbf{J}$) and nonclassical ($\mathbf{G}$) tautomers Luo and Crabtree in 1990 synthesized a set of mononuclear complexes ($\mathbf{C}$ – $\mathbf{J}$) of d-metal ($\mathbf{Me}$). $\mathbf{B}$ was used as an initial compound, 4.098 g of which can be obtained by the addition reaction from 3.273 g $\mathbf{Me}\mathrm{O_n}$ and the equimolar mass of $\mathrm{NaO}_n$ at $250\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The synthesis of complexes was as follows: $\mathbf{B}$ was dissolved in alcohol, then 6.210 g of $\ce{(CH3)2C6H5P}$ ($\ce{Me2PhP}$) were added, and after addition of concentrated HCl the reaction mixture was boiled during 18 hours with reflux condenser and the orange $\mathbf{C}$ was formed (m g, yield 80%). CO was bubbled at boiling through the alcohol solution of $\mathbf{C}$ until 4.408 g of yellow $\mathbf{D}$ was formed (50% yield). To the etheric solution of $\mathbf{D}$ $\ce{LiAlH4}$ was added and boiled with reflux condenser during 40 hours till yellow $\mathbf{E}$ ($w_\mathrm{Me} = 29.50$; $w_\mathrm{P} = 14.73$; $w_\mathrm{O} = 2.53\%$) was formed, which contained ligand $\mathbf{L}$, but no $\ce{Cl-}$. $\mathbf{E}$ was dissolved in $\ce{CH2Cl2}$, then it was protonated using $\ce{HBF4}$ at 208 K and a daffodil solution of equilibrium mixture of $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{J}$ was obtained, which has conductivity close to $\ce{LiAlH4}$. The complexes $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{G}$ have c.n. = 7, and in $\mathbf{J}$ c.n. = 8. For $\mathbf{G} \rightleftarrows \mathbf{J}$ Luo and Crabtree obtained $\Delta H^0 = -4.6\,\mathrm{kJ/mole}$, $\Delta S^0 = -10\,\mathrm{J/mol\cdot K}$.

1. Determine $\mathbf{Me}$ and define the formula of $\mathbf{B}$.

2. Determine the formulae of nonelectrolytes $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{E}$, if they are complexes $\mathbf{Me}$(3+), and calculate m.

3. Determine $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{J}$, if the IR-spectrum of $\mathbf{J}$ contains $1832\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ band, and $\mathbf{G}$ – two bands 1838 and $2692\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ (the IR-spectra of $\mathrm{K}\mathbf{MeL}_4$ contain band $1828\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, and $\mathbf{L}_2$ – $4159\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$).

4. Write the reaction equations of complex formation.

5. Calculate $\Delta G^0$ and the composition of the equilibrium mixture $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{J}$ in mol.% at 208 K, considering that $\Delta H^0$ and $\Delta S^0$ do not depend on temperature.

6. Propose the structure of intermediate fragment at the transition of $\mathbf{G}$ to $\mathbf{J}$, if the bond distances: L–L in $\mathbf{G}$ – 0.084; in $\mathbf{J}$ – 0.160; in the intermediate 0.138 nm.

7. Draw MO diagram for $\mathbf{L}_2$ and the overlapping of orbitales in $\mathbf{G}$ in bond formation of $\mathbf{Me}$ with ligands containing $\mathbf{L}$.

problems.problem:
Problem 5 (Inorganic Chemistry section, problem 2). [A family of halogen compounds]

Learning without reflection is a waste, Reflection without learning is dangerous — Confucius (551 – 479 BC)

The halogens atoms have a large gamma of possible oxidation numbers which leads to a great diversity of compounds and interesting structures. However, it is important to remember that some halogens compounds could be very toxic and explosive and it is very important to pay attention working and exploring the halogen compounds.

Compounds $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{Y}_{1,2}$, $\mathbf{Z}$ have the same qualitative composition. The oxidation number of central atom is growing in the row $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{Y}$, $\mathbf{Z}$. The compound $\mathbf{B}$, which was obtained by fluorination of the binary compound $\mathbf{A}$ ($\omega_\mathrm{F}$ = 34.86%), could produce compounds $\mathbf{Y}_1$ ($\omega_\mathrm{F}$ = 52.53%) or $\mathbf{Y}_2$ by partial hydrolysis. Pure compound $\mathbf{Y}_2$ could be obtained by three methods: a) by the reaction of compound $\mathbf{A}$ with the brownish- yellow gas $\mathbf{C}$, b) by the fluorination of yellow-orange gas $\mathbf{D}$ or c) by the hydrofluorination of dark red liquid $\mathbf{E}$. Binary compounds $\mathbf{C}$ – $\mathbf{E}$ have the same qualitative composition. One of the elements of compounds $\mathbf{C}$ – $\mathbf{E}$ is the same that the central atom of $\mathbf{X}$-$\mathbf{Z}$ molecules. The oxidation number of this element is growing in a row $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{E}$; moreover the oxidation number of this element is the same in $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ compounds. The synthesis of $\mathbf{C}$ from simple compound $\mathbf{F}$ and mercury (II) oxide is one of the few methods to obtain compound $\mathbf{C}$ in a pure state.

The compound $\mathbf{Y}_2$ was oxidized by strong oxidizing agent as $\ce{PtF6}$ to obtain equimolar quantity of salts $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{H}$. During the action of nitryl fluoride on $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{H}$ it was obtained respectively $\mathbf{Y}_2$ and new product $\mathbf{Z}$.

All discussed reactions are represented on the scheme. Take into account that it is not always given all by-products.

1. Determine all unknown compounds. Take into account that the synthesis of $\mathbf{Y}_2$ from $\mathbf{C}$ is going through the formation of unstable compound $\mathbf{X}$ which disproportiones quickly on equimolar quantities of $\mathbf{Y}_2$ and $\mathbf{A}$.

2. Write all equations of reactions given on the scheme.

3. Give the structural formulae and the hybridization of central atom for compounds $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$, cations $\mathbf{G}$, $\mathbf{H}$, and also for $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{Y}_{1,2}$, $\mathbf{Z}$.

4. Explain why the liquid $\mathbf{E}$ conducts the current.

5. Write the hydrolysis reactions of $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{E}$ compounds.

problems.title: [Inorganic analogues of carbon compounds]
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (Inorganic Chemistry section, problem 3). [Inorganic analogues of carbon compounds]

Carbon is like gold: it is shiny and precious. (Russian national proverb)

In inorganic chemistry there are substances with physical and chemical properties similar to organic. In this problem, you are invited to meet with three groups of compounds are examples of such similarities.

Carbon has a large number of allotropic modifications – graphite, diamond, fullerenes, graphene, carbon nanotubes. Inorganic binary compound $\mathbf{E}$ can form a structure similar to all of the above. $(\mathbf{E})_3$ is isoelectronic to $\ce{C6}$ cell in the graphite structure. The ratio of elements of the $\mathbf{E}$ is 1: 1. At a pressure of 7 GPa and a temperature of $1500\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ $\mathbf{E}$ becomes crystal structure of diamond. The hardness of $\mathbf{E}$ is less than diamond, but more durable, heat-resistant and chemically resistant, so it is widely used for polishing steel.

The elements included in the $\mathbf{E}$, also form $\mathbf{M}$ – a colorless liquid, which is also called "inorganic benzene" for a similar smell, and a ring structure with a system of delocalized π-electrons. Due to the difference in the electronegativities of the atoms included in the $\mathbf{M}$, it is more reactive in addition reactions compared to benzene.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2016-2-6-fig1.png

1. Determine the $\mathbf{M}$ and $\mathbf{E}$, write the reaction equations represented in the scheme.

2. Write a reaction that may occur in the processing of steel diamond polish wheels and reduce their service.

In addition to the $\mathbf{E}$ some transition metals compounds have structures similar to allotropic carbon modifications too. The most active work is carried out to obtain "inorganic graphene" based on them for the creation of optoelectronic semiconductors. Binary substance $\mathbf{N}$ was one of the first, which managed to obtain monolayers with a similar layer structure of graphene. Obtaining a given structure of $\mathbf{N}$ occurs in several stages. At first, thermal decomposition of $10^{-3}$ mol of ammonium salt $\mathbf{B}$ produces 178 mL of gas with a sharp odor at $90\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and a pressure of 1 atm, 1.008 g of the oxide $\mathbf{O}$ of hexavalent metal $\mathbf{C}$ (the oxygen content of the oxide $\mathbf{O}$ is 33.3% mass) and 89 mL water vapor. Further, monolayers $\mathbf{N}$ are formed after the interaction between $\mathbf{O}$ and hydrogen sulfide in a stream of hydrogen at $400\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

3. Determine the $\mathbf{N}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$. What side product will be formed if the reaction is carried out without hydrogen? Write the equation of this reaction.

After 20 days after the closing ceremony of the 49th International Mendeleev Olympiad an article was published in Science Journal by scientist from MIT about how to obtain inorganic ion $\mathrm{P}_x\mathrm{N}_y^-$ – analogue of cyclopentadienyl anion (Cp). According to the mass spectrum of $\mathrm{P}_x\mathrm{N}_y^-$, his mass number m/z = 104 was defined.

4. a) determine the molecular formula of the anion, if it is known that two signals are observed in the spectrum of $^{15}$N NMR, $x$ and $y$ are integers number;

b) draw resonance structures of $\mathrm{P}_x\mathrm{N}_y^-$.

In addition to $\mathrm{P}_x\mathrm{N}_y^-$ there are other inorganic compounds containing phosphorus, nitrogen and sulfur and being isoelectronic to Cp;

c) write three molecular formula of the respective cation, anion and molecule.

5. a) write a Hückel rule for aromaticity for organic substances;

b) determine the number of $\pi$-electrons in $\mathbf{M}$ and $\mathrm{P}_x\mathrm{N}_y^-$.

problems.title: [Ortho- and para-hydrogen]
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (Physical Chemistry section, problem 1). [Ortho- and para-hydrogen]

The molecules $\mathbf{A}_2$, formed by nuclides with $i \neq 0$, have nucleus isomers. The nuclei of atoms $\mathbf{A}$ with odd number of nucleons are described by Fermi – Dirac statistics and ortho-isomer ($o$-$\mathbf{A}_2$) has odd total spin $I$ ($I = \Sigma i$), para-isomer ($p$-$\mathbf{A}_2$) – even.

1. Give $I$ for $o$-$\ce{H2}$ and $p$-$\ce{H2}$. Indicate the orientation of spins by arrows.

For the reaction $p$-$\ce{H2} \rightleftarrows o$-$\ce{H2}$ the equilibrium constant $K = \chi_\mathrm{o}/\chi_\mathrm{p} = f(T)$ at low $T$ (see table), and at high – $K \neq f(T)$. $K$ = 2.98 (400 K); 3.00 (500 K); 3.00 (600 K).

2. Derivate the equation $\ln K = A + B/T$ if $\Delta G^0 = -RT\ln K$ and $\Delta G^0 = \Delta H^0 - T\Delta S^0$. Using $\chi_i$, calculate $A_\mathrm{av}$ and $B_\mathrm{av}$ and fill the gaps in the table.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} T,\ \mathrm{K} & 20 & 30 & 40 & 60 & 100 \\ \hline \chi_\mathrm{p},\ \text{mol.\%} & & 97.0 & & 65.8 & 38.6 \\ \hline K & 1.89\cdot10^{-3} & & 0.127 & & \end{array}$$

3. Calculate $\Delta H^0$ and $\Delta S^0$, considering, that they are independent of $T$.

In 2010 J. Ingues proposed three step scheme for the reaction at high $T$. At the first step $p$-$\ce{H2}$ (1 atm, 600 K, $V$, $\chi_\mathrm{p} = 1$) transforms to $o$-$\ce{H2}$ (1 atm, 600 K, $V$, $\chi_\mathrm{o} = x$) and $p$-$\ce{H2}$ (1 atm, 600 K, $V$, $\chi_\mathrm{p} = 1 - x$) with entropy $\Delta S_\mathrm{I} = 9.2x\,\mathrm{J/K}$. At the second step $o$-$\ce{H2}$ and $p$-$\ce{H2}$ mix together and entropy equals $\Delta S_\mathrm{II} = -R[x\ln x + (1-x)\ln(1-x)]$. At the third step – $T$ changes and $\Delta S_\mathrm{III} = C_V\cdot\ln(T/600)$.

4. Give the condition, at which $K \neq f(T)$ if $d\ln K/dT = \Delta H^\circ/RT^2$.

5. Calculate $\Delta S_\mathrm{I+II} = \Delta S_\mathrm{I} + \Delta S_\mathrm{II}$ for $x$ = 0.6, 0.7, 0.8 and 0.85. Build the graph $\Delta S_\mathrm{I+II} = f(x)$, determine $x$ for $\Delta S_\mathrm{I+II}$ = max, calculate for it $K_0$ and compare with given in the condition $K$ for high $T$.

6. Determine the minimal $T$, at which the scheme works, if entropy change in the reaction and at change of $T$ are equal and $C_V = 20.9\,\mathrm{J/mol\cdot K}$.

The nuclei of atoms $\mathbf{A}$ with even number of nucleons are described by Bose – Einstein statistics and $o$-$\mathbf{A}_2$ has even spin, and $p$-$\mathbf{A}_2$ – odd. The value $\chi_i$ is proportional to the possible conditions $2I + 1$.

7. Give $I$ for ortho- and para-isomers of deuterium ($o$-$\ce{D2}$ and $p$-$\ce{D2}$).

8. Calculate the maximal possible content of isomers for $\ce{H2}$ and $\ce{D2}$ and show the stable ones.

Problem 8 (Physical Chemistry section, problem 2). [Two- and three-dimensional Born–Haber cycles]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2016-2-8-fig1.png

The Born – Haber cycle based on Hess law, is a convenient graphical method for studying the thermodynamics of chemical reactions. Such a cycle for the formation reaction of the chloride of metal $\mathbf{A}$, which comparing two ways of this process – from simple substances (I) and an ideal gas of ions of the substance (VII), is shown in left figure. The latter passes through the stages: sublimation of $\mathbf{A}$ (II), ionization of $\mathbf{A}$ (III, IV), dissociation of chlorine (V), ionization of chlorine atoms (VI).

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{Stage} & \text{II} & \text{III} & \text{IV} & \text{V} & \text{VI} \\ \hline \text{Energy, kJ/mol} & 164 & 549 & 1064 & 243 & -349 \end{array}$$

Upon dissolution of the carbonate of metal $\mathbf{A}$ in the hydrochloric acid 69.7 kJ of heat is absorbed $\mathbf{A}\mathrm{CO_3(s)} + \mathrm{2HCl(l)} = \mathbf{A}\mathrm{Cl_2(sol)} + \mathrm{CO_2(g)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)}$. $\mathbf{A}\mathrm{Cl_2}$ crystallizes from the solution as hexahydrate. For it's decomposition with the aim of obtaining anhydrous salt it is necessary to spend 344.3 kJ of heat.

1. a) Calculate the lattice energy ($E_\mathrm{lat}$) $\mathbf{A}\mathrm{Cl_2}$. b) Write the composition of the particles corresponding to state $\mathbf{B}$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{Compound} & \mathbf{A}\mathrm{CO_3(s)} & \mathbf{A}\mathrm{Cl_2(sol)} & \mathrm{H_2O(l)} & \mathrm{H_2O(g)} & \mathbf{A}\mathrm{Cl_2\cdot6H_2O(s)} & \mathrm{CO_2(g)} \\ \hline \Delta_\mathrm{f}H^0_{298},\ \mathrm{kJ/mol} & -1220 & -805.4 & -285.8 & -241.8 & -2624 & -393.5 \end{array}$$

Metal $\mathbf{A}$ with a density of $2.54\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$ has a cubic face-centered crystal lattice. The radius of atom $\mathbf{A}$ is equal to $r$ = 0.217 nm.

2. a) Express $r$ through the parameter $a$ of the unit cell. b) Determine $\mathbf{A}$.

The above cycle describes the processes that occur at a fixed temperature, pressure and other parameters. Building of three-dimensional Born – Haber cycle with changeable external parameters allows to predict the most thermodynamically favored route of complex chemical reactions. In the following figure, as an example, a diagram of a simple reaction between metal $\mathbf{A}$ and hydrochloric acid at three different temperatures of 348, 298 and 170 K (the scale of energy is not respected) is shown. At 170 K chlorine and hydrochloric acid are the liquids.

Description: $Q_T \equiv \Delta_\mathrm{r}H^0_T$; $\mathbf{a} = \Delta_\mathrm{f}H^0_{348}(\mathrm{HCl,\ g})$; $\mathbf{c} = [\Delta H_\mathrm{lat} + 3RT]$; $\mathbf{f} = [C_p(\mathrm{A^{2+}},\ \mathrm{g}) + 2C_p(\mathrm{Cl^-},\ \mathrm{g}) + 2C_p(\mathrm{H_2},\ \mathrm{g})]\Delta T$; $\mathbf{g} = [C_p(\mathbf{A}\mathrm{Cl_2},\ \mathrm{s}) + C_p(\mathrm{H_2},\ \mathrm{g})]\Delta T$; $\mathbf{h} = \Delta_\mathrm{f}H^0_{298}(\mathrm{HCl,\ g}) = -92.3\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$; $\mathbf{j} = [\Delta H_\mathrm{lat} + 3RT]$; $\mathbf{o} = \Delta_\mathrm{f}H^0_{170}(\mathrm{HCl,\ l})$; $\mathbf{b} = -2976\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$, $\mathbf{e} = 4.39\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$; $\mathbf{d} = 4.171\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$; $\mathbf{k} = -92.0\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$; $\mathbf{l} = -92.09\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$; $\mathbf{n} = -76.97\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$.

3. Write the expression of the energies of processes $\mathbf{b}$, $\mathbf{d}$, $\mathbf{e}$.

4. Determine $\Delta_\mathrm{r}H^0_{348}$, $\Delta_\mathrm{r}H^0_{298}$, $\Delta_\mathrm{r}H^0_{170}$ (kJ/mol), using three-dimensional Born – Haber cycle and the data from paragraph 1

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{Compound} & \mathrm{HCl(g)} & \mathrm{HCl(l)} & \mathrm{Cl_2(l)} & \mathrm{Cl_2(g)} & \mathrm{H_2(g)} & \mathbf{A}\mathrm{Cl_2(s)} \\ \hline C_p,\ \mathrm{J/mol\cdot K} & 29.16 & 152.6 & 67.03 & 33.84 & 28.83 & 54.42 \end{array}$$

problems.title: [Kinetic scheme of a heterogeneous catalytic reaction]
problems.problem:
Problem 9 (Physical Chemistry section, problem 3). [Kinetic scheme of a heterogeneous catalytic reaction]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2016-2-9-fig1.png

In the physical chemistry no way exist for prediction of activity of catalyst in certain reaction based on its physico-chemical properties meaning that there is no "general theory of catalysis". For the prediction understanding of mechanism of catalytic reaction is required. To determine the mechanism one often carry out kinetic investigation of the reaction and establish the kinetic scheme approximately. The scheme consist of sequence of intermediate compounds and by-products obtaining in the course of reaction.

A schematic diagram of reactor used in heterogeneous catalytic reactions, widespread in the industry, is illustrated in the Figure. For quantitative determination of activity of catalyst conversion $C$ of the raw (mole fraction of reacted raw with respect to raw fed), selectivity $S(X)$ on target product $\mathbf{X}$ (mole fraction of $\mathbf{X}$ with respect to all products) and yield $Y(X)$ of product $\mathbf{X}$ are in common use.

1. Derive the equation for yield on product $\mathbf{X}$ using conversion of raw and selectivity on product $\mathbf{X}$.

For the investigation of kinetic scheme one vary contact time of catalyst with raw. Since it is easier to change WHSV (weight hourly space velocity, or feed rate) without changes in catalyst weight, one does it by this way. After that one analyze distribution of products depending on feed rate and suppose kinetic scheme of reaction.

2. Derive the equation for contact time ($\tau$, s) of catalyst with raw using catalyst weight ($m$, kg), its bulk density ($\rho$, $\mathrm{kg/m^3}$) and raw feed rate ($V$, L/min).

Investigation of catalytic conversion of A into B was carried out in continous flow reactor at $200\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The catalyst weight was 0.5 kg in all experiments and its bulk density was $1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$. Feed rate was changed in the range of 1 – 30 L/min. It was discovered that by-products $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{E}$ are obtained beside $\mathbf{B}$ and unreacted $\mathbf{A}$. For each feed rate yield of $\mathbf{A}$ – $\mathbf{E}$ products was calculated and given in the Table.

3. a) Calculate contact time of catalyst with raw for each feed rate value based on the data given in the Table; b) Reveal kinetic scheme of reaction using the dependence of yields on contact time. Consider all the transformations as irreversible first-order reactions.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} V,\ \mathrm{L/min} & Y(\mathbf{B}),\ \% & Y(\mathbf{C}),\ \% & Y(\mathbf{D}),\ \% & Y(\mathbf{E}),\ \% \\ \hline 30.0 & 0 & 2 & 0 & 9 \\ \hline 5.0 & 2 & 18 & 4 & 26 \\ \hline 2.5 & 6 & 22 & 9 & 38 \\ \hline 1.5 & 17 & 15 & 12 & 46 \\ \hline 1.0 & 40 & 5 & 2 & 50 \end{array}$$

4. a) Calculate conversion of $\mathbf{A}$ for all feed rate values (fill the Table in the answer sheet); b) Which function describes the dependence of conversion of $\mathbf{A}$ on contact time if only irreversible $\mathbf{A}$ to $\mathbf{B}$ transformation occurs over the catalyst?

5. Calculate conversion of $\mathbf{A}$ at $210\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and feed rate 5 L/min under the same other conditions. Consider activation energy of $\mathbf{A}$ to $\mathbf{B}$ conversion as 50 kJ/mol.

problems.title: [Interpolyelectrolyte complexes of chitosan]
problems.problem:
Problem 10 (Life Sciences and Polymers section, problem 1). [Interpolyelectrolyte complexes of chitosan]

Macromolecules of polyelectrolytes (PE) contain groups capable of dissociation in aqueous solutions. PEs can interact with other charged species via the ion exchange mechanism.

1. Draw structures of the repeating units of the polymers listed in the Answer Sheet. Of these, select a pair of PEs that react with one another in their aqueous solution to form an interpolyelectrolyte complex.

A water-soluble polymer chitosan is prepared via hydrolysis of natural polymer chitin (see the structure in the Answer Sheet) in the presence of acetic acid.

[The list of polymers for question 1 and the structure of chitin are printed only in the Answer Sheet, which is not available.]

2. Draw a scheme of chitin hydrolysis yielding chitosan and determine the amount of charged groups per one chitosan macromolecule if its molecular mass is 492310 g/mol and the average molecular mass of the repeating unit is 164.10 g/mol.

Chitosan exists in the form of polycation in acidic aqueous solutions, thus being capable of interacting with negatively charged species. For example, the interaction of aqueous solutions of chitosan and compound $\mathbf{A}$ (50.00 wt.% C, 5.60 wt.% H, 44.40 wt.% O) gives a loose precipitate of the interpolyelectrolyte complex. The freezing point of 1 wt% aqueous solution of sodium salt of $\mathbf{A}$ (the cryoscopic constant of water is of $1.86\,\mathrm{kg\cdot deg/mol}$) equals $-0.208\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

3. Determine the gross formula and molecular mass of $\mathbf{A}$. Take that dissociation of $\mathbf{A}$ is complete.

Yellow substance $\mathbf{B}$ prepared by interaction of ammonium molybdate(VI) with phosphoric acid in an excess of nitric acid (not a redox reaction) belongs to a special class of compounds containing a polyvalent anion of complex structure. The corresponding acids behave similar to polyacids and are capable of the interacting with polybases to form interpolyelectrolyte complexes.

4. a) Write down the equation of formation of $\mathbf{B}$. Note that drying of $\mathbf{B}$ to constant mass at $150\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ leads to the residue with the metal content of 61.36% and phosphorus content of 1.65%.

b) How many anions of $\mathbf{B}$ per the chitosan molecule (see i. 2) are found in the stoichiometric polycomplex? If you have failed to give the answer in i. 2, take $N$ as the number of ionogenic groups in the chitosan molecule.

Enthalpy of the reactions of polyelectrolyte complex formation being close to zero, these reactions occur owing to high positive entropy change, which is due to the release of small ions initially located in the vicinity of the polyion into the bulk solution.

5. Indicate the low-molecular weight ions released in the course of interaction of:

a) the polyelectrolytes chosen in i. 1

b) chitosan and the acid corresponding to $\mathbf{B}$. If you have failed to give the answer in i. 1, 2, or 4, give your own examples of the interacting polyelectrolytes (no more than two pairs), drawing their structures in the Answers Sheet.

The entropy increase owing to the small ions release into the bulk solution is partially compensated by an unfavorable change of entropy due to binding of the polyions (these polymers initially distributed in the entire volume of the reaction mixture are later found in the precipitate of the insoluble complex). Note that entropy is related to the number of microscopic states of the system which provide for its macroscopic state.

6. Arrange the following compounds in the increasing order of their tendency towards complex formation with chitosan: tribromoacetic acid $\mathbf{C}$, acid $\mathbf{A}$, and the acid corresponding to $\mathbf{B}$. Determine the element with the highest content (by mass) in the dried precipitate of the chitosan complex with a mixture of these acids (each of three acids taken in an excess with respect to the stoichiometric ratio).

problems.title: [Sous-vide cooking]
problems.problem:
Problem 11 (Life Sciences and Polymers section, problem 2). [Sous-vide cooking]

To the authors of task 6 at IChO-2015, big connoisseurs of freshly baked bread

Cooking in vacuum (fr. sous-vide) is a method when meat or vegetables are placed into a sealed airtight plastic bag and simmered long at relatively low and controlled temperature, usually in a water-bath. The method is characterized by a number of advantages. In the case of meat slabs (usually boiled or braised) the correct choice of temperature (~$60\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) provides for complete transformation of muscular collagen (fibrillar protein, the major component of connective tissue) into gelatin with maximum retention of the meat succulence.

1. Write down (in general form) the reaction equation of collagen transformation into gelatin.

The color of beef is by 90-95% due to the protein of myoglobin, specifically to the ratio of its three forms differing in the corresponding ion and/or the ligand bound:

• Myoglobin (Mb), containing $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ and water molecule;
• Oxymyoglobin ($\mathrm{MbO_2}$), containing $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ and oxygen molecule;
• Metmyoglobin (MMb+), containing $\ce{Fe^{3+}}$ and water molecule.

Fresh-killed meat is of deeper color inside the slab as compared to its external parts, and is practically free of MMb+. Due to precise temperature control and uniform heating of the slab, Sous-vide allows cooking ideal steaks with different degree of doneness accordingly differing in the meat color.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \textbf{The degree of steak doneness} & \textbf{Color} & \textbf{Temperature of cooking, }{}^\circ\mathbf{C} \\ \hline \text{Extra-rare or Blue (bleu)} & \text{Rich red} & 46\text{–}49 \\ \hline \text{Medium (demi-anglais)} & \text{Pink in the center, more read towards the outer parts} & 60\text{–}65 \\ \hline \text{Well done (bien cuit)} & \text{Grey-brown} & 71 \\ \hline \text{Overcooked (trop cuit)} & \text{Black} & >100 \end{array}$$

2. Determine the prevailing myoglobin form (Mb, $\mathrm{MbO_2}$ or MMb+) at each of the mentioned above degrees of steak doneness.

3. What other process developing in the course of sous-vide cooking of meat can be behind the taste difference depending on the degree of steak doneness.

Conventional meat panbroiling leads to typical dish smell, color and taste. This is mostly due to the formation of Maillard reaction products (occurs at t > $150\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$). Impossibility of Maillard reaction is one of sous-vide drawbacks disappointing gourmands.

Compound $\mathbf{X}$ providing a dish with the smell of butter is formed via Maillard reaction. The formula of $\mathbf{X}$ can be represented as $\mathrm{C}_p\mathrm{H}_q\mathrm{O}_r$. It obeys two following equations: $p + q + r = 12$ (1) and $p\cdot q\cdot r = 48$ (2).

4. Derive the molecular formula of $\mathbf{X}$ if the mass content of hydrogen in $\mathbf{X}$ exceeds 7%.

5. Draw the structural formula of $\mathbf{X}$ if it is known that $\mathbf{X}$ contains 2 types of C atoms and one type of H and O atoms each.

On the other hand, sous-vide allows avoiding a number of toxic products, such as $\mathbf{Y}$ ($\ce{C3H5NO}$). $\mathbf{Y}$ is formed by Maillard reaction from amino acid asparagine and a 1,2-dicarbonyl compound (e.g., 3-deoxyglucosone, a D-glucose derivative) according to the hereunder scheme (reaction equations at all stages):

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2016-2-11-fig1.png

It is known that $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{L}$ are binary substances.

6. Draw the 3-deoxyglucosone structure in Fischer projection.

7. Draw the structural formulae of $\mathbf{A}$ – $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{G}$, $\mathbf{L}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$.

Compound $\mathbf{Z}$ is an $\mathbf{Y}$ metabolite. Being a mutagen $\mathbf{Z}$ is a hazardous substance for man. $\mathbf{X}$ transformation into $\mathbf{Z}$ is a single-stage enzymatically catalyzed process. $\mathbf{Z}$ contains 36.75% O and 41.38% C by mass and has an asymmetric C atom.

problems.title: [Poisons and antidotes]
problems.problem:
Problem 12 (Life Sciences and Polymers section, problem 3). [Poisons and antidotes]

All things are poison and nothing is without poison; only the dose makes a thing not a poison. Paracelsus

Toxicology deals with poisons and mechanisms of their action. Poisons are substances causing disruption of vital activity of an organism when present in it in relatively small doses (thus, as little as 100 ng of particular protein toxins and as much as 200 g of sodium chloride lead to fatal case in man). Since, a human being is in every day contact with various chemicals, knowledge of their toxicological properties as well as the first aid measures in the case of intoxication is vitally important. Substances easing the influence of poisons on organisms are referred to as antidotes.

1. Names of some substances ($\mathbf{1}$ – $\mathbf{5}$) often met in chemical labs are given in the hereunder table. Penetration of these substances into organisms leads to intoxication. Based on their chemical properties, correlate in the Answer Sheet each substance with the structure of its antidote ($\mathbf{A}$ – $\mathbf{E}$).

$$\begin{array}{c|l} \mathbf{1} & \text{white arsenic} \\ \hline \mathbf{2} & \text{methanol} \\ \hline \mathbf{3} & \text{hydrofluoric acid} \\ \hline \mathbf{4} & \text{lead sugar} \\ \hline \mathbf{5} & \text{carbon monooxide} \end{array}$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2016-2-12-fig1.png

Cyanide is the favorite poison in detective novels, cytochrome c oxidase (an iron-containing enzyme of the respiratory chain) being its target in organisms. In the case of intoxication with potassium cyanide or vapors of hydrocyanic acid, it is needed to open an ampoule with isoamyl nitrite and let the sufferer inhale its vapors.

2. Draw the structure of isoamyl nitrite and write down the sequence of equations of three reactions occurring in blood, which explain the antidote action. Remember that hemoglobin is one of the blood components! Denote the unessential part of organic molecules as R.

After applying the first aid measures described above, sodium thioisulfate is administered to the patient intravenously.

3. Write down the equation of this final detoxication stage if two sulfur-containing particles are its low molecular weight products.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2016-2-12-fig2.png

Overdosing of drugs often leads to intoxication. Even well known preparations like $\mathbf{P}$ can be dangerous if overdosed. The toxicity of $\mathbf{P}$ is due to the product of its single stage enzymatic transformation $\mathbf{P1}$ (9.40% N by mass) with one of antidotes ($\mathbf{A}$ – $\mathbf{E}$) being a reagent in this transformation.

4. Deduce the structure of $\mathbf{P1}$ if the number of the carbon atoms is not changed in the transformation from $\mathbf{P}$.

$\mathbf{PA}$ ($\ce{C5H9NO3S}$) obtained by a single stage synthesis from a canonical amino acid acts as an antidote in the case of such intoxication. $\mathbf{PA}$ is a diprotic acid with $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$ values of 3.2 and 11.2; its solutions decolorize $\ce{KI3}$ solution. $\mathbf{PA}$ enters into the reaction of nucleophilic addition to $\mathbf{P1}$, aromatic substance $\mathbf{P2}$ being the sole reaction product.

5. Deduce the structures of $\mathbf{PA}$ and $\mathbf{P2}$, write down the reaction schemes.

Overdosing of $\mathbf{P}$ leads to liver injury induced by $\mathbf{P1}$.

6. Exhaustion of what biologically important molecules is behind the liver injury? Choose the correct variant in the Answer Sheet.

[The variants for question 6 are printed only in the Answer Sheet, which is not available.]

$\mathbf{X1}$ is one of the most potent (still slow-response) poisons. This is a three-element metal salt. Penetration of as low as 1 ng of this substance into the organism can turn out to be lethal. The intoxication manifests in gradual development of sickness, head-ache, hyperthermia, blood effusion, gastrointestinal upset and mental breakdown. The numbers of atoms in the formula unit of $\mathbf{X1}$ are a geometrical progression, the total sum of the numbers does not exceed 15, and the mass content of carbon equals 16.2%.

7. Do calculations to determine $\mathbf{X1}$ and write down the reaction equation explaining its toxicity. Write down the reaction of thermal decomposition of $\mathbf{X1}$.

Problem 1. [Bacterial biodegradation of PET]

"I'll be back"
Terminator T-800

Paying tribute to my constant co-author

Plastic pollution is defined as accumulation of plastic products in the environment producing a negative impact on animal and human habitats. This problem is among the most vital challenges facing humanity nowadays. Surprisingly, sometimes nature itself offers assistance, such as bioremediation. Proteins are composed of α-amino acid residues linked together by peptide bonds between carboxylic and amino groups. Ladderanes form very interesting class of hydrocarbons, unusual structural fragment of which is present in the Nature in lipids of planctomycetes that realize anammox, i.e. ANaerobic AMMonium OXidation. It was a serious breakthrough in chemistry with the discovery of electricity: the birth of electrochemistry, the discovery of new elements, etc. In 1807 Humphry Davy obtained the metals $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ by electrolysis of their molten compounds. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2017-1-6-fig1.png

H. Davy (1778 – 1829)

During the combustion of $\mathbf{B}$ on the air the orange substance $\mathbf{C}$ ($\omega(\mathrm{O}) = 45\%$) is formed, the combustion of $\mathbf{A}$ causes the formation of other oxygen-compound $\mathbf{H}$ ($\omega(\mathrm{O}) = 41\%$) of pale yellow colour. Both $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{H}$ compounds are used for the regeneration of oxygen in submarines and spacecraft. This process is based on the interaction between $\mathbf{C}$ and carbon dioxide, which leads to the formation of $\mathbf{D}$ and oxygen. Evaporating of the solution obtained by reacting of $\mathbf{D}$ with hydrochloric acid, the compound $\mathbf{E}$ may be prepared, which is the starting material for obtaining $\mathbf{B}$ by the reaction with $\mathbf{A}$ in industry. The latter reaction of obtaining $\mathbf{B}$ is used even more in industry than electrolysis. This process takes place in a stainless steel column: the melt of $\mathbf{E}$ moves downwards and the vapour of $\mathbf{A}$ moves down up. The vapour of $\mathbf{B}$ sublimes and condenses in the refrigerator. Upon cooling the solution obtained by adding $\mathbf{C}$ to the acidified by sulfuric acid solution of aluminum sulfate is obtained well-faceted colorless crystals $\mathbf{F}$. At the reaction of the solution of $\mathbf{F}$ with sodium perchlorate, a white precipitate $\mathbf{G}$ is obtained, which is one of the few poorly soluble metal compounds of $\mathbf{B}$.

problems.title: [Portland cement clinker]
problems.problem:
Problem 7. [Portland cement clinker]

There are many types of cement, but the most widespread one is Portland cement. It is mostly (more than 90%) composed of ground clinker, whose approximate composition is given in the table below. The properties of Portland cement are commonly defined by two calcium silicates, $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$, in the clinker. The mass fractions of calcium in $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ are 52.66% and 46.54% respectively. The first row of the table below contains the international designations (in cement chemistry) of various components of the clinker. In reality, clinker comprises approximately 2–3% mass. of minor components (oxides of potassium, sodium, phosphorus, manganese, sulfur, hydrogen, etc. in bound states, which come from the source materials), but we will not consider them in this problem.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{Designation} & & & \mathbf{C_4AF} & \mathbf{C_3A} & \mathbf{M} \\ \hline \text{Composition} & \mathbf{X} & \mathbf{Y} & \ce{Ca4Al2Fe2O10} & \ce{Ca3Al2O6} & \ce{MgO} \\ \hline \omega,\% & 62.0 & 16.0 & 8.50 & 12.0 & 1.50 \end{array}$$

The raw materials used in making the clinker are various natural minerals: limestone (calcite), clay (kaolinite $\ce{Al2O3*2SiO2*2H2O}$), periclase (MgO), iron ore ($\ce{Fe2O3}$) and quartz sand. All the aforementioned minerals contain $\ce{SiO2}$ as an impurity, which is 8.50% of the minerals by mass. In addition to $\ce{SiO2}$, iron ore also contains 4.10% of $\ce{Al2O3}$, and clay contains 4.60% of $\ce{Fe2O3}$. All the starting materials are mixed together in required proportions and calcined (heated when exposed to air) at $1500\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in special rotating furnaces to obtain clinker. After cooling and grinding, the clinker is mixed with gypsum (under these conditions, it partially dehydrates to form gypsum plaster, also known as plaster of Paris) to produce Portland cement. The amount of gypsum added must be so that the mass fraction of sulfur oxide (VI) in the final product is 3.00%.

Because the compositions of natural raw materials used in the process are not constant in a real industrial process, the ratios of the components used in making clinker must constantly be adjusted. The properties of Portland cement are most affected by the ratio of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$, which depends on the ratio of $\ce{SiO2}$, $\ce{Al2O3}$ and $\ce{Fe2O3}$ in the clinker. In order to control this ratio, the Lime Saturation Factor (LSF) is used, which is computed by using the mass fractions of the aforementioned oxides in the clinker. The Lime Saturation Factor is computed as follows:

$$\mathrm{LSF} = \frac{\omega(\ce{CaO})}{2.80\cdot\omega(\ce{SiO2}) + 1.18\cdot\omega(\ce{Al2O3}) + 0.650\cdot\omega(\ce{Fe2O3})}$$

The LSF characterizes the ratio between quantities of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$, as well as the degree of binding of CaO in the clinker. If LSF = 1, then only $\mathbf{X}$ is present and there is no $\mathbf{Y}$, and if LSF>1, then $\mathbf{X}$ and unbound CaO are present. The magnitude of LSF is used to confirm that the composition of cement is standardized, and will behave in a predictable manner.

1. Determine the chemical formulas of X and Y and give their international designations.

2. Calculate the masses of all components needed to produce 100 tons of Portland cement.

3. Calculate the mass fractions of all oxides in Portland cement.

4. Calculate LSF for Portland cement of the above composition. Show your calculations.

In all calculations, use atomic masses rounded to the nearest integer. The final answers should have at least three significant figures.

problems.title: [Photocatalytic water splitting on titanium dioxide]
problems.problem:
Problem 8. [Photocatalytic water splitting on titanium dioxide]

Hydrogen is a promising renewable energy source. One of the ways of production of hydrogen is photocatalytic decomposition of water. The mechanism of the process is presented in figure. Titanium dioxide can serve as an example of such a photo-catalyst. Under light excitation with photon energy, greater than the band gap of the semiconductor ($E_\mathrm{g}$) electrons transfer to the conduction band, leaving holes (h+) in the valence band. The efficiency of the process decreases because of rapid recombination of the pairs $\mathrm{e^-}$–$\mathrm{h^+}$. For charge separation the catalyst is doped by transition metals.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2017-1-8-fig1.png

1. Choose the metals in the table, addition of which can improve the efficiency of photo-catalytic decomposition of water.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \text{Ion} & E^0(\ce{Me^{n+}}/\ce{Me}),\ \mathrm{V} & \text{Ion} & E^0(\ce{Me^{n+}}/\ce{Me}),\ \mathrm{V} \\ \hline \ce{Fe^{3+}} & -0.037 & \ce{Pt^{2+}} & 1.12 \\ \hline \ce{Mn^{2+}} & -1.19 & \ce{Ru^{2+}} & 0.445 \\ \hline \ce{Co^{2+}} & -0.28 & \ce{Cu^{2+}} & 0.521 \\ \hline \ce{Ce^{3+}} & -2.34 & \ce{Ag+} & 0.7996 \end{array}$$

In the systems, having particles smaller than 100 nm, size effects are often observed – dependence of physical-chemical properties of substances from the size of the particles. Dependence of the band gap on the size of nanoparticles for an oxide semiconductor is expressed by the formula

$$E_\mathrm{g}(R) = E_\mathrm{g0} + \frac{a}{R^2} - \frac{b}{R},$$

where $E_\mathrm{g0}$ – band gap of the bulk phase, $\mu = m_\mathrm{e}^*\cdot m_\mathrm{h}^*/(m_\mathrm{e}^* + m_\mathrm{h}^*)$ – reduced mass of the effective masses of electron ($m_\mathrm{e}^*$) and a hole ($m_\mathrm{h}^*$), $\varepsilon_0$ – electric constant, $\varepsilon$ – dielectric permittivity, $e$ – electron charge, $R$ – radius of the particle, $a = h^2/8\mu$, $b = 1.8e^2/4\pi\varepsilon\varepsilon_0$.

2. a) Calculate the band gap energy value for $\ce{TiO2}$ nanoparticles with $R = 2\,\mathrm{nm}$, if $E_\mathrm{g0} = 3.0\,\mathrm{eV}$, $\varepsilon = 184$, $\mu = 0.74\,m_\mathrm{e}$; b) In what direction shifts the wavelength of radiation which initiates conductivity, in case of nanoparticles, compared with bulk phase? c) Calculate the effective mass of electrons and holes if $m_\mathrm{e}^* = 12.5\,m_\mathrm{h}^*$.

Efficiency of photocatalytic hydrogen production can be estimated with the quantum yield $\varphi$ – ratio of the number of the "effective" electrons ($n_\mathrm{e}$) to the number of photons ($n_\mathrm{p}$) generated by a light source per time unit.

3. Calculate the quantum yield $n_\mathrm{e}/n_\mathrm{p}$ (%). The maximum rate of hydrogen formation for this catalyst $V_\mathrm{max} = 5.6\,\mathrm{\mu mol/min}$, light source power $P = 67\,\mathrm{mW}$, light wavelength 421 nm.

Kinetics of the reactions, occurring on the photocatalyst surface, can be described using Langmuir – Hinshelwood model:

$$\ce{A + Z <=>[K_A] AZ ->[k] P + Z}$$

where Z – adsorption centers, A – organic substrate, P – product of the reaction, $K_\mathrm{A}$ – adsorption constant, $k$ – reaction rate constant. The rate of hydrogen in this reaction is defined as $W(\ce{H2}) = kn_\mathrm{A}$, where $n_\mathrm{A} = \dfrac{K_\mathrm{A}C_\mathrm{0A}}{1 + K_\mathrm{A}C_\mathrm{0A}}$ – degree of surface coverage. After linearization of the curve $W(\ce{H2})$ the equation $y = 3.27 + 1.78x$ was obtained (see figure).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2017-1-8-fig2.png

4. a) Determine, to what variables correspond $x$ and $y$ on the graph; b) calculate $k$ and $K_\mathrm{A}$.

Physical constants: $h = 6.63\cdot10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\cdot s}$, $N_\mathrm{A} = 6.02\cdot10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$, $c = 3\cdot10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\cdot s^{-1}}$, $1\,\mathrm{eV} = 1.6\cdot10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$, $m_\mathrm{e} = 9.1\cdot10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\cdot10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F/m}$, $e = 1.6\cdot10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$.

Problem 1 (Inorganic Chemistry section, problem 1). [Anion HEOn– and its polynuclear derivatives; Fremy's experiment]

problems.title: [Dodecahydrododecaborate and carborane superacids]
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (Inorganic Chemistry section, problem 2). [Dodecahydrododecaborate and carborane superacids]

The most compounds containing the chemical bond B–H have a high reactivity. However, there are exceptions to this rule. In 1955 on the basis of theoretical calculations it was shown that dodecahydrododecaborate(2–) anion and isoelectronic structures should be high stable. Formally, this anion can be considered a derivative of a non-existent dodecaboran (14). In 1960, the corresponding salt of sodium dodecahydrododecaborate(2–) was first obtained, which really had enviable stability. The matter turned out to be in the spatial structure of an anion having a regular highly symmetric structure. All the boron atoms in it are located at the vertices of the regular polyhedron with 12 vertices (icosahedron), and each of the 20 faces is an equilateral triangle with boron atoms at its vertices. It is believed that the icosahedron of boron atoms and isoelectronic structures have spatial aromaticity and this explains their high stability.

1. Give the formulas and names of three really existing substances, the molecules of which have a spatial framework, which is a polyhedron, in the vertices of which atoms of one chemical element connected by chemical bonds are located.

2. Calculate the multiplicity of each chemical bond in the dodecahydrododecaborate (2–) anion.

The dodecahydododecaborate (2–) anion is not destroyed at $95\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in concentrated aqueous solutions of alkali (NaOH) and acids (HCl). The corresponding acid (A) isolated from the aqueous solution is slightly stronger than sulfuric acid.

3. Calculate the mass fraction of boron in acid A, give your calculations.

To obtain the sodium dodecahydrododecaborate(2–) can be as follows. In the first step, sodium octahydrotriborate(1–) is obtained from sodium tetrahydroborate(1–) and diborane (6). In the second step the pyrolysis of the product at $180\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is carried out and the final product is obtained.

4. Draw the structural formula of the anion product of the first step synthesis.

5. Give the reaction equations for the preparation of sodium dodecahydrododecaborate(2–).

If in the dodecahydrododecaborate(2–) anion one boron atom is replaced by a carbon atom without disturbing the three-dimensional aromaticity of the system, a very stable anion (B) is obtained, which made it possible to synthesize one of the most powerful superacids (C) at the present time. To produce it, the anion B (as a cesium salt) is first chlorinated with an excess of $\ce{SO2Cl2}$ (in argon atmosphere) in a suitable solvent, whereby all hydrogen atoms in the B-H bonds are replaced by chlorine atoms. The obtaining salt can be converted to a superacid (C), called carborane acid, as a result of several additional steps.

6. Give the formula of carborane acid C.

Carborane acid is capable of protonating methane at room temperature. In this case, its solid stable salt is formed with methyl carbocation. When this salt is washed on the filter with cyclohexane at room temperature, the product is contaminated with another solid salt.

7. Give a scheme of the reaction proceeding at hexane washing and explain the structure of the salt, which is formed.

In 2013, the super acid D was obtained even more strongly than carborane.

8. What is the mass fraction of boron in D? Show your calculations.

(The nomenclature of boron compounds with hydrogen includes the designation of the number of boron atoms in the Latin numerals with the addition of borane and the addition at the end in parentheses of the Arabic number of hydrogen atoms, for example, $\ce{B4H10}$ – tetraborane(10). For anions the number of hydrogen atoms and the number of boron atoms indicate with the addition of borate, and the charge of the anion indicates in parentheses at the end. For example, $\ce{Ca[B3H8]2}$ – octahydrotriborate (1–) of calcium).

problems.title: [Binary compounds of two elements X and Y]
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (Inorganic Chemistry section, problem 3). [Binary compounds of two elements X and Y]

Two chemical elements ($\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$) combine to form different binary compounds, which could be gases, liquids or even solids. Nine of these binary compounds ($\mathbf{A}$ – $\mathbf{I}$) are descripted on this scheme:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2017-2-3-fig1.png

The treatment of compound $\mathbf{A}$ by the solution of sodium hypochlorite (Raschig processes) is used to obtain colorless liquid $\mathbf{B}$, which it is not possible to obtain by the direct interaction of simple compounds of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$. This liquid $\mathbf{B}$ is mostly used as a racket fuel. $\mathbf{B}$ could be obtained from the white compound $\mathbf{K}$: the reaction of 0.72 g of $\mathbf{K}$ with the excess of sodium hypochlorite solution, gives 0.384 g of liquid $\mathbf{B}$. The hydrolysis of the compound $\mathbf{K}$ produces two gases $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{W}$ ($\rho_\mathbf{W} = 1{,}964\,\mathrm{g/L}$ at the normal conditions). The volatile and caustic liquid $\mathbf{C}$ was obtained for the first time by the reaction of $\mathbf{B}$ with the acid $\mathbf{L}$. The using of excess of the acid $\mathbf{L}$ leads to the further oxidation of compound $\mathbf{C}$ with the formation of equimolar quantities of gases $\mathbf{Y}$, $\mathbf{Z}$ and water. The compound $\mathbf{C}$ is a basic when reacts with strong acids (for example the formation of salt $\mathbf{M}$) or it is an acid when reacts with the compounds $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ giving salts $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{E}$ respectively. For synthesis of 0.855 g of the salt $\mathbf{E}$ by the sequences $\mathbf{B} \rightarrow \mathbf{C} \rightarrow \mathbf{E}$, 0.864 g of compound $\mathbf{B}$ have to be used taking into account that the yield on two stages is respectively 80% and 95%. By gradual heating at low pressure the unstable compound $\mathbf{F}$ could be obtained from the liquid $\mathbf{C}$. The compound $\mathbf{F}$ transforms to the yellow gas $\mathbf{G}$ and reacting with oxygen forms the acid $\mathbf{L}$ even at the room temperature. The compound $\mathbf{F}$ could exist in the singlet and triplet states. The compound $\mathbf{H}$ was never obtained in a pure state, but it exists as salt $\mathbf{H}\cdot\mathrm{HCl}$ and it is a side product of Raschig processes. The compound $\mathbf{H}\cdot\mathrm{HCl}$ is the only product of the reaction $\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{J}$. The covalent compound $\mathbf{I}$ is the derivative of the compound $\mathbf{G}$, which exists in different isomeric forms. The heating of $\mathbf{I}$ leads to the isomerization reaction giving the salt $\mathbf{D}$, or to the formation of $\mathbf{B}$ with emission of one equivalent of gas $\mathbf{Y}$. The compounds $\mathbf{K}$ and $\mathbf{H}$ are similar structurally.

1. Decipher binary compounds $\mathbf{A}$ – $\mathbf{I}$ and also compounds $\mathbf{J}$ – $\mathbf{M}$, $\mathbf{W}$, $\mathbf{X}$ – $\mathbf{Z}$.

2. Write the equations of all described reactions.

3. Write Lewis structures for singlet and triplet states of compound $\mathbf{F}$. Give a particle (molecule or atom) which is isoelectronic to $\mathbf{F}$.

4. Why $\mathbf{H}\cdot\mathrm{HCl}$ could be a side product during the Raschig processes? Write down the equation of this chemical reaction.
