Problem 3 (Life Sciences and Polymers section, problem 3). [The Ketone energy drink and meldonium]

In 2017, the HVMN Company commercialized Ketone, a novel energy drink based on the compound $\mathbf{X}$ and designed to improve the athletes’ results.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2018-2-3-fig1.png

If taken, $\mathbf{X}$ (54.53% C, 9.15% H, 36.32% O by mass) is hydrolyzed in small intestine affording the compounds $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$. $\mathbf{A}$ is absorbed into blood, which is followed by its metabolic transformation into $\mathbf{B}$ in liver. The corresponding reaction equations are given hereunder (E1 – E3 are enzymes):

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2018-2-3-fig2.png

1. Deduce the molecular and all possible structural formulae of $\mathbf{X}$ meeting the above conditions including $\mathbf{A}$ transformation into $\mathbf{B}$ and having the minimum possible molecular mass.

2. How would your previous answer change if you get to know that the molar fraction of C is higher by 6.7% than that of O in $\mathbf{B}$. Be sure to support your new answer by calculations.

$\mathbf{B}$ can be enzymatically oxidized in blood into the compound $\mathbf{D}$, which decomposes either enzymatically or non-enzymatically to the compound $\mathbf{E}$ containing hydrogen atoms of only one type. The corresponding reaction equations are given hereunder (E4 and E5 are enzymes):

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2018-2-3-fig3.png

3. Deduce the structural formulae of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{X}$.

Let us suppose you have decided to use Ketone to run marathon (42.2 km) having in mind to demonstrate a very good time of 2 hours 20 minutes (neglect energy consumption on all other process but running). It is known that:

• The derivative of $\mathbf{D}$ with co-enzyme A reacts with free co-enzyme A affording the sole product $\mathbf{J}$. Complete oxidation of $\mathbf{J}$ in mitochondria leads to energy elaboration of 360 kJ/mol;
• The efficiency of $\mathbf{J}$ oxidation in man approaches two thirds of the theoretical maximum;
• Running on a plane road requires 40 kJ/min at the speed of 8 km/h, 65 kJ/min at 11 km/h, and 95 kJ/min at 19 km/h.

4. Calculate the number of the Ketone bottles (shown on the picture) you will need provided $\mathbf{X}$ is your only energy source when running. If you have failed to deduce the structure of $\mathbf{X}$, show your work in general form.

Some bacteria (e.g. Ralstonia eutrophus) produce a biopolymer using $\mathbf{B}$ as the only starting substance.

5. Draw the structural formula of the biopolymer.

6. In the Answer Sheet, choose only one correct statement explaining the reason behind the biopolymer synthesis by microorganisms.

It is quite probable that $\mathbf{X}$ will be once included in the list of the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA), similarly to what has happened to the pharmaceutical Meldonium in 2015.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2018-2-3-fig4.png

High-performance liquid chromatography-mass selective detection assay with electrospray ionization used for Meldonium determination in an athlete’s urine requires the compound $\mathbf{Y}$ (a zwitter-ion; 25.0% C, 8,3% O, and 8.3% N by moles) as an internal standard. The molar mass of $\mathbf{Y}$ is within the range of 100 to 200 g/mol. The mass-spectrum of the solution prepared by mixing aliquots of $\mathbf{Y}$ solution and urine containing Meldonium is characterized by five pronounced peaks with $m/z$ 58, 59, 60, 61, and 62 (other peaks are also found in the spectrum).

7. Deduce possible structures of $\mathbf{Y}$, show calculations supporting your answer.

The mixed doubled curling team representing Olympic Athletes from Russia had to return the bronze medal won at the Olympic Games in PyeongChang, since 8.1 mcg/mL (probe A dated 02.02.2018) and 5.7 mcg/mL (probe B dated 03.02.2018) were found in urine of one curler. It is also known that no Meldonium was detected in his urine in the probe dated 22.01.2018. According to the WADA database, the absolute maximum Meldonium content ever found in an athlete’s urine is 1428 mcg/mL.

8. Based on the above information, choose only one correct statement in the Answer Sheet.

problems.title: Organometallic reagents
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (Organic Chemistry section, problem 1). Organometallic reagents

Organometallic compounds $\mathbf{I}$–$\mathbf{V}$ based on the element $\mathbf{X}$ are important reagents in organic chemistry. Most of them are derivatives of $\mathbf{X}$, containing cyclopentadienyl (Cp or $\ce{C5H5}$) ligand, which can be obtained from binary compound $\mathbf{A}$. Thus, by treating the liquid chloride $\mathbf{A}$, which intensively emits fumes when exposed to air, with sodium cyclopentadienide in tetrahydrofuran (THF), the bright red crystals of compound $\mathbf{I}$ ($w(\mathbf{X}) = 19.23\%$) are formed. $\mathbf{I}$ is the starting compound for other cyclopentadienyl complexes of $\mathbf{X}$ synthesis. When $\mathbf{I}$ is reduced with magnesium in the atmosphere of CO, the maroon complex $\mathbf{II}$ ($w(\mathbf{X}) = 20.45\%$) is formed. But if $\mathbf{I}$ is reduced with zinc in tetrahydrofuran, the green crystals of compound $\mathbf{III}$ ($w(\mathbf{X}) = 22.42\%$) can be extracted, which exists in free form as a dimer. The treatment of $\mathbf{I}$ with the excess of MeLi leads to the formation of $\mathbf{IV}$ ($w(\mathbf{X}) = 23.00\%$), and if $\mathbf{I}$ is reacted with 2 equivalents of $\ce{Me3Al}$ in toluene, the binuclear complex $\mathbf{V}$ ($w(\mathbf{X}) = 16.82\%$) is formed, which has 2 tetrahedral metallic centers connected to each other with two bridging ligands. In this reaction the compound $\mathbf{Y}$ ($w(\mathrm{Al}) = 29.17\%$) is also formed and methane releases. The compounds $\mathbf{IV}$ and $\mathbf{V}$ are precursors of highly reactive molecule $\mathbf{Z}$, what is more, it can be generated from $\mathbf{IV}$ by heating or from $\mathbf{V}$ by pyridine treatment.

1. Determine the element $\mathbf{X}$ and compound $\mathbf{A}$. Draw structural formulae of complex compounds $\mathbf{I}$–$\mathbf{V}$, molecule $\mathbf{Z}$ and compound $\mathbf{Y}$. In complexes $\mathbf{I}$–$\mathbf{V}$ and compounds $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{Z}$ indicate the formal oxidation state of element $\mathbf{X}$.

The diversity of mentioned reagents possibilities can be illustrated with the following schemes:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2018-2-4-fig1.png

2. Draw the structural formulae of compounds $\mathbf{B}$ – $\mathbf{F}$, if it is known, that compound $\mathbf{B}$ is thermodynamically more stable isomer, and $\mathbf{C}$ is chiral. Correlate the reagents $\mathbf{II}$ – $\mathbf{V}$ with their role in organic transformations (olefinating reagent, deoxygenative reagent, one-electron reductant).

problems.title: [Sumanene]
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (Organic Chemistry section, problem 2). [Sumanene]

Sumanene (from Hindi "flower") is a conjugated hydrocarbon $\mathbf{X}$ ($\ce{C21H12}$), which can be considered as a fullerene fragment. Attempts to synthesize $\mathbf{X}$ began in 1993 with the pyrolysis of the corresponding substance $\mathbf{A}$. However, during this sythesis, only compounds $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ were isolated with a low yield.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2018-2-5-fig1.png

1. Give the structures of sumanene $\mathbf{X}$ and compounds $\mathbf{A}$ – $\mathbf{C}$

Successful synthesis of Sumanene $\mathbf{X}$ was realized only 10 years later, in 2003. The synthesis began from hydrocarbon $\mathbf{F}$, which has 3 signals in the $^1$H NMR spectrum (int 2:1:1) and 3 signals in the $^{13}$C NMR spectrum. In his turn, hydrocarbon $\mathbf{F}$ is obtained by the reaction of equimolar addition of hydrocarbon $\mathbf{D}$ and gas $\mathbf{E}$ ($w_\mathrm{C} = 92.3\%$). A further step was the modification of $\mathbf{F}$ to form a bifunctional compound $\mathbf{G}$, which, under the action of copper (I) salts, gives a mixture of hydrocarbons $\mathbf{H1}$ and $\mathbf{H2}$ in a ratio of 1:3 with the brute formula $\ce{C21H18}$. The major $\mathbf{H2}$ isomer under olefin metathesis conditions leads to hydrocarbon $\mathbf{J}$. At the same time, the minor isomer of $\mathbf{H1}$ under similar conditions leads to compound $\mathbf{I}$, which during oxidation gave the desired sumanene $\mathbf{X}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2018-2-5-fig2.png

2. Give the structural formulae of compounds $\mathbf{D}$ – $\mathbf{J}$.

The sumanene which was synthetized, possesses a number of interesting properties. Thus, there are two doublets in the $^1$H NMR spectrum of sumanene at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ at 3.42 and 4.71 ppm, which, when heated to $140\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, merge into a wide signal. For a more detailed study of this phenomenon, a deuterated derivative of $\mathbf{Y}$ was obtained according to the scheme given below. Compound $\mathbf{Y}$ at room temperature in the NMR spectrum gave two singlets at 3.42 and 4.71 ppm. with equal intensities, which indicated the existence of $\mathbf{Y}$ in two forms. In addition, it was found that the transition frequency between these two forms was $0.066\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $0.007\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ at 318 K and 298 K, respectively.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2018-2-5-fig3.png

3. Draw the structural formulae of $\mathbf{Y}$ and anion $\mathbf{Z}$.

4. Show the structures of two forms of $\mathbf{Y}$, which has the corresponding signals in NMR: 3.42 and 4.71 ppm

5. Calculate the activation energy to pass from one form of $\mathbf{Y}$ to another.

problems.title: Halomon: chemist vs algae
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (Organic Chemistry section, problem 3). Halomon: chemist vs algae

In 1992, substance $\mathbf{X}$ later called halomon, was isolated from the red alga Portieria hornemannii. The compounds surprisingly possessed a unique ability of selective toxicity to certain cancer cells lines. Combustion of 1.00 g of halomon leads to formation of 24.9 mmol of $\ce{CO2}$, 12.5 mmol of water and a mixture of hydrogen halides, which under $\ce{AgNO3}$ treatment gave 2.01 g of precipitate. In the mass spectrum of halomon there is a bizarre signal in the region with an unusual distribution of isotopic peaks. In addition, it was found that halomon in nature is synthesized from β-myrcene -– an acyclic monoterpene and has a 3-S, 6-R-configuration. However, despite the preliminary success of the compound testing, its low natural concentration and difficulties with the breeding of Portieria hornemannii, forced the project to stop. He was rescued by synthetic chemists in 2000 by the synthesis of racemic halomon from β-myrcene according to the scheme presented below. But the synthesis did not solved the problem due to its low selectivity and accessibility only to the racemic compound. On the step of compound $\mathbf{B}$ formation, the main product was compound $\mathbf{B1}$ with a terminal double bond, as well as impurity $\mathbf{B2}$ as a mixture of cis / trans isomers. At the final step of halomon formation, the byproduct $\mathbf{D}$ was isolated, which appears halomon diastereomer.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2018-2-6-fig1.png

1. Determine the empirical formula of halomon, the answer is confirmed by calculation.

2. Give the structural formula of the natural enantiomer of halomon.

3. Decipher compounds $\mathbf{A}$ – $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{B1}$, $\mathbf{B2}$ and $\mathbf{D}$.

The final synthetic victory over halomon chemists celebrated in 2015, developing a preparative method for the synthesis of the natural enantiomer. The method was based on the enantioselective halogenation of allylic alcohols according to the general scheme given below. Thus, the dual use of this method using different enantiomers of the catalyst starting from hydroxylated β-myrcene in 6 preparative steps with high yield and optical purity.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2018-2-6-fig2.png

4. Decipher compounds $\mathbf{E}$ – $\mathbf{I}$.

problems.title: [Water softening with EDTA]
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (Analytical Chemistry section, problem 1). [Water softening with EDTA]

Salts of ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA, $\ce{H4Y}$) form very stable $\mathrm{MetY}^{(4-x)-}$ complexes with many $\mathrm{Met}^{x+}$ metal ions. EDTA is used in textile, paper, paint, and other industries to soften industrial water, as well as in analytical chemistry. EDTA is a weak acid, its dissociation constants are as follows: $K_1 = 1.0\cdot10^{-2}$; $K_2 = 2.1\cdot10^{-3}$; $K_3 = 6.9\cdot10^{-7}$; $K_4 = 5.5\cdot10^{-11}$.

1. There is water of medium hardness without precipitate (calcium concentration: 2.9 mM, magnesium: 2.0 mM, total concentration of all forms of carbonic acid: 1.8 mM).

a. Calculate the volume of a 1 M solution of EDTA disodium salt $\ce{Na2H2Y}$, which should be added to $1\,\mathrm{m^3}$ of such water to reduce its hardness (Ca + Mg) to 1.5 mM.

b. What are the concentrations of forms of carbonic acid in such water, if its pH equals 6.3? Dissociation constants of carbonic acid: $K_1 = 4.5\cdot10^{-7}$, $K_2 = 4.8\cdot10^{-11}$.

c. The maximum possible pH of the water described in the problem situation is determined by the precipitation of insoluble carbonates. Calculate this value, assuming the system is in equilibrium. Solubility products: $K_\mathrm{S}(\ce{CaCO3}) = 3.8\cdot10^{-9}$, $K_\mathrm{S}(\ce{MgCO3}) = 2.1\cdot10^{-5}$.

2. To $1\,\mathrm{m^3}$ of the same water as in item 1, 30.0 L of a 1.00 M solution of EDTA disodium salt were added.

a. In which reactions will ions $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ and $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ and the salts of carbonic acid enter upon the addition of the softening agent? Write down the reaction equations.

b. Let the initial pH of the water be equal to 6.3. Estimate the pH value of this water after the addition of EDTA, considering complexation complete.

c. Complete complexation of magnesium and calcium with EDTA occurs at pH ≥ 8.0. What amount of 1M alkali solution should be added to $1\,\mathrm{m^3}$ of the softened water, so that its pH reaches this value? Consider that $\ce{CO2}$ does not evaporate from the solution.

problems.title: [A glass pH electrode and the acid HnA]
problems.problem:
Problem 8 (Analytical Chemistry section, problem 2). [A glass pH electrode and the acid HnA]

At the beginning of the 20th century, the ability of glass membranes to selectively react to hydrogen ions was discovered, which triggered the development of ion-selective electrodes. A combined glass ion-selective electrode measures the potential difference between the inner solution with a known pH value and the test solution. This difference in potentials is given by formula (1), where $S$ is the angle of inclination of the electrode function, theoretically equal to 2.3RT/F (in practice this value may be different):

$$\Delta E = \mathrm{S}\cdot\log\frac{[\ce{H+}]_\mathrm{test}}{[\ce{H+}]_\mathrm{inner}} \qquad (1)$$

1. The electrode potential was measured in two buffer solutions with pH 4.00 and 7.00, obtaining the potential differences of 0.2094 V and 0.0352 V, respectively. Calculate the pH of the inner electrode solution and parameter S.

Under real-world conditions, the alkali metals cations can interfere with the measurement of the proton concentration, since the electrode glass is partially selective to these cations. This selectivity is determined by the selectivity constant $k_\mathrm{H/M}$, and the potential difference is determined by formula (2):

$$\Delta E = \mathrm{S}\cdot\log\frac{[\ce{H+}]_\mathrm{test} + k_\mathrm{H/M}\cdot[\ce{M+}]}{[\ce{H+}]_\mathrm{inner}} \qquad (2)$$

2. Determine the selectivity constant $k_\mathrm{H/Na}$ of the electrode, knowing that the error in measuring the concentration of $\ce{H+}$ ions for 0.2018 M solution of NaOH is 2018%.

Below is given a distribution diagram of all forms of inorganic acid $\mathrm{H_nA}$. This electrode was used to measure the pH value of two solutions: 0.100 M $\mathrm{Na_nA}$ and an acid salt 0.100 M $\mathrm{Na}_m\mathrm{H}_{n-m}\mathrm{A}$. The obtained potential values are –0.2376 and 0.1803 V respectively.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2018-2-8-fig1.png

3. According to the diagram, what is the basicity of the acid?

4. What forms of acid does correspond to each of four curves?

5. Find all acidity constants for $\mathrm{H}_n\mathrm{A}$ acid.

Quantitatively, the A ions were determined by precipitation of a silver salt: 20.0 mL of a solution prepared by dissolving 1.53 g of $\mathrm{H_nA\cdot0.5H_2O}$ in a 100 mL flask was titrated with 0.500 M $\ce{AgNO3}$ solution in the presence of chromate and sodium acetate. The volumes spent in the titration were as follows: 12.15; 12.20; 12.75 mL.

6. What is the role of chromate and acetate during the titration? Write the corresponding chemical reactions.

7. Find the molecular mass of $\mathrm{H}_n\mathrm{A}$ and it formula, if A consists of two elements.

problems.title: [Systematic qualitative analysis of a mixture of four chlorides]
problems.problem:
Problem 9 (Analytical Chemistry section, problem 3). [Systematic qualitative analysis of a mixture of four chlorides]

The systematic qualitative analysis of the mixture of four chlorides is described below. All salts are white crystalline solids with no crystallization water. To an aqueous solution of this sample the solution of complex acid $\mathbf{A}$, containing 47.60 wt% of a platinum group metal, was added. Precipitate 1 thus obtained was then separated. To remaining solution 1, the solution of double acetate $\mathbf{B}$, containing 41.64 wt% uranium and some amount of zinc, was added. A yellow precipitate of triple salt hexahydrate $\mathbf{C}$ was formed, with mass percentages of metals of 1.49%, 46.43% and 4.25%. This confirmed the presence of metal $\mathbf{X1}$ salt in the sample.

Precipitate 1 was washed, dried, calcined and dissolved in water. The resulting solution 2 was separated from metallic precipitate 2, and the solution (in hydroiodic acid) of complex acid $\mathbf{D}$, containing bismuth and 70.74 wt% of iodine, was added to it. The obtained precipitate of compound $\mathbf{E}$ confirms the presence of metal $\mathbf{X2}$ salt in the sample. Mass fractions of $\mathbf{X2}$ and iodine in $\mathbf{E}$ are related as 1:2.865, and the anion has a structure of two octahedra sharing a common face with an atom of bismuth in the center of each octahedron.

The remained solution 3 was several times evaporated with $\ce{HNO3}$, the residue was dissolved in water, and $\ce{NaNO2}$, $\ce{Bi(NO3)3}$ and $\ce{AgNO3}$ were added to resulting solution 4. The formation of yellow precipitate $\mathbf{F}$ indicated the presence of $\mathbf{X3}$ in the sample. $\mathbf{F}$ contains an ion of bismuth coordinated with six equal ligands, and mass fractions of nitrogen and oxygen in $\mathbf{F}$ are 11.00 and 25.14%, respectively.

Finally, after separation of precipitate $\mathbf{F}$, the reagent for cations of metal $\mathbf{X4}$ was added to resulting solution 5. This reagent is a sodium salt $\mathbf{G}$ containing 14.59 wt% of cobalt as a part of complex anion. Herewith in the presence of remaining silver nitrate in the solution, a yellow precipitate of compound $\mathbf{H}$ with mass percentage of $\mathbf{X4}$ 15.01% was formed.

Note: use all the relative atomic masses of elements accurate to a hundredth.

1. Determine the composition of the initial mixture of salts, metals $\mathbf{X1}$–$\mathbf{X4}$ and write down the formulae of compounds $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{H}$. Confirm the answers with calculations.

2. Draw the structural formulae of complex anions of $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{E}$.

3. Write down the equations of all reactions mentioned.

problems.title: [Binding energies: proton affinity, a metal carbonyl and hydration of Me2+]
problems.problem:
Problem 10 (Physical Chemistry section, problem 1). [Binding energies: proton affinity, a metal carbonyl and hydration of Me2+]

The binding energy ($E$) can be calculated in a direct way, using the $\Delta H^\circ_x$ for the reaction $\mathrm{M(g)} + a\mathrm{L(g)} = \mathrm{ML}_a\mathrm{(g)}$ if enough data is available for the thermodynamic cycle. This is possible when calculating the affinity for the proton ($A_\mathrm{p}$).

1. Calculate the $A_\mathrm{p}$ $\ce{NH3(g) + H+(g) = NH4+(g)}$ and $E_\mathrm{av}$ of the N–H bond in $\ce{NH4+}$ if $\Delta_f H^0$ are as follows (kJ/mol): –46.0 ($\ce{NH3}$), 664 ($\ce{NH4+}$), 218 (H), 473 (N), and the ionization potential $\ce{H = H+ + e-}$ is equal to $I = 13.6\,\mathrm{eV}$.

The data are also sufficient for $\mathbf{Me}\mathrm{(g)} + a\mathrm{CO(g)} = \mathbf{Me}\mathrm{(CO)}_a\mathrm{(g)}$, since $\Delta_f H^0$(kJ/mol) are known: –110 (CO), –732 ($\mathbf{Me}\mathrm{(CO)}_a$), 424 ($\mathbf{Me}$). For the carbonyl $W_\mathrm{C} = 30.6\%$ by weight.

2. Determine $\mathbf{Me}$ and carbonyl. Describe the structure of carbonyl by the valence bond method (VB).

3. Calculate the $E_\mathrm{av}$ of the $\mathbf{Me}$–CO bond and explain its difference from the real (251 kJ/mol), indicating the process included in the VB method and that was not taken into account during the calculation. Calculate its $(\Delta H^0)^*$.

In the case of $\mathbf{Me}^{2+}$(g) cations, the data for the direct method are insufficient. Therefore, first $\Delta H^\circ_x$ of hydration is calculated, and from this value $\Delta H^\circ_x$ for other ligands is obtained. To calculate the $\Delta H^\circ_x$ of hydration from the standpoint of the electrostatic theory, it is considered that it is equal to the potential energy ($U$) of a system containing 6$\ce{H2O}$ at the vertices of octahedron and $\mathbf{Me}^{2+}$ at the center of it. This energy (kJ/mol) includes the cation-dipole attraction (–1395), the cation-induced dipole attraction (–897), as well as the dipole-dipole (513) and the cation-dipole (407) repulsions.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2018-2-10-fig1.png

4. Calculate the value of $U$ and the average bond energy $E_\mathrm{av}$ for $\mathbf{Me}$–$\ce{H2O}$

A more accurate calculation of $E_\mathrm{av}$ can be performed in a semi-empirical way using the experimental enthalpies (kJ/mol): $\ce{H2O(l) = H2O(g)}$ ($\Delta H^0_\mathrm{v} = 44.0$); $\mathbf{Me}^{2+}\mathrm{(g)} + 6\ce{H2O(l)} = \mathbf{Me}\mathrm{(H_2O)_6^{2+}(aq)}$ ($\Delta H^0_\mathrm{g} = -1958.1$) and the calculated Born heat of hydration $\mathbf{Me}\mathrm{(H_2O)_6^{2+}(g)} = \mathbf{Me}\mathrm{(H_2O)_6^{2+}(aq)}$: $\Delta H^0_\mathrm{B} = -N_\mathrm{A}e^2z^2\left(1 - 1/\varepsilon - T(\partial\ln\varepsilon/\partial T)_P/\varepsilon^2\right)/4\pi\varepsilon_0 r = -kz^2(1 - 1/\varepsilon + 0.356T/\varepsilon^2)/r$, where $e = 1.602\cdot10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$; $\varepsilon_0 = 8.854\cdot10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F/m}$; $N_\mathrm{A} = 6.02\cdot10^{23}$; $z$ – cation charge; $r$ – the distance between the cations. The entropy is $\Delta S^0_\mathrm{B} = -0.356kz^2/\varepsilon^2 r$.

5. Calculate $\Delta H^0_\mathrm{B}$, $\Delta S^0_\mathrm{B}$, $\Delta G^0_\mathrm{B}$, if $\varepsilon = 78$ at 298 K, $r(\mathbf{Me}^{2+}) = 0.83\,\mathrm{\mathring{A}}$, diameter $\ce{H2O}$ $D = 2.76\,\mathrm{\mathring{A}}$

6. Calculate $\Delta H^0_x$ for $\mathbf{Me}^{2+}\mathrm{(g)} + 6\ce{H2O(g)} = \mathbf{Me}\mathrm{(H_2O)_6^{2+}(g)}$ and $E_\mathrm{av}$ for the bond $\mathbf{Me}$–$\ce{H2O}$.

There are noticeable differences in the values of $E_\mathrm{av}$ obtained from the electrostatic model and the semi-empirical method for all electronic configurations except $d^0$, $d^{10}$, $d^5$ (weak field).

7. Specify the name of the energy, which is not included in the calculation of the electrostatic model.

problems.title: [ESR spectroscopy in radiation chemistry]
problems.problem:
Problem 11 (Physical Chemistry section, problem 2). [ESR spectroscopy in radiation chemistry]

Electron spin resonance (ESR) spectroscopy is a powerful method to study paramagnetic species (these containing one or several unpaired electrons), widely used in physics, chemistry, and biology. Intensity of the ESR signal is proportional to the number of unpaired electrons in the sample, therefore quantitative measurements using ESR method are possible without additional data on the substance, in contrast to other spectroscopy methods.

1. Which of the species listed in the Answer Sheet (OH, H, $\ce{H2}$, $\ce{TiCl3}$, $\ce{H[CuCl2]}$, $\ce{VOSO4}$, $\ce{ZnCl2}$), can be observed by means of ESR?

ESR is of special importance in radiation chemistry (a branch of science studying the processes occurring under the action of ionizing radiation). The irradiation induces the formation of radicals, structure and concentration of which can be determined by means of ESR. To answer this and following questions, use the definitions and reference data given in the end of the task.

2. Calculate the steady-state concentration of radicals formed upon irradiation and indicate whether they can be detected by means of ESR. Assume that the radicals disappear only via bimolecular reaction between them. Radiation-chemical yield $G$ = 2 radicals/100 eV, dose rate $I = 10\,\mathrm{J/kg\cdot s}$, sample volume $10\,\mathrm{\mu L}$, sample density $\rho = 1\,\mathrm{g/mL}$, rate constant of radicals recombination $k = 10^{10}\,\mathrm{L/mol\cdot s}$, temperature 298 K, sensitivity of the ESR spectrometer $10^{11}$ spins in a sample.

To study the short-living radicals, the measurements are performed on cooling, and the radicals recombination can be neglected for.

3. Estimate the radiation-chemical yield of radicals at 77 K if the measured intensity of the ESR signal is 0.0366, dose rate $10\,\mathrm{J/(kg\cdot s)}$, irradiation duration 20 min, sample density $\rho = 0.98\,\mathrm{g/mL}$, intensity of ESR signal of the reference sample (150 mg of $\ce{CuCl2*2H2O}$) 52.4. The ampoule with the sample is a cylinder with diameter $d = 4\,\mathrm{mm}$ and height $l = 1.5\,\mathrm{cm}$.

4. UV absorption spectrum of the irradiated sample (see i. 3) was recorded. The detected absorbance in the absorption maximum was $A = 1.33$. Calculate the molar absorptivity $\varepsilon$ if only a single type of radicals is stabilized in the sample, and the absorption is due to the presence of these radicals. Optical path goes along the ampoule diameter. If you have failed to solve i. 3, take the number of radicals in the sample equal to $5\cdot10^{17}$.

5. Calculate the minimum concentration of the radicals described in ii. 3–4 that can be detected by means of a) UV spectroscopy (the lowest reliably measurable absorbance $A = 0.01$) and b) ESR spectroscopy (detector sensitivity $10^{11}$ spins in a sample). If you have failed to solve i. 4, take $\varepsilon = 1500\,\mathrm{L/mol\cdot cm}$.

The radicals formation is important in view of radiation-chemical transformations of polymers. For polymers prone to crosslinking under irradiation, the gel dose term is used; this is a minimum dose of the radiation sufficient for the transformation of the sample in a single cross-linked macromolecule.

6. Calculate the gel dose for polyethylene ($M = 100000\,\mathrm{g/mol}$). Radiation-chemical yield of radicals $G$ = 3 radicals/100 eV. Account for the processes of the radicals formation under irradiation and their recombination.

Absorbed dose (unit J/kg) is the energy of radiation absorbed per a mass unit. Dose rate is the dose absorbed by the substance per a time unit. Radiation-chemical yield is the number of species appeared or decayed in the sample upon absorption of 100 eV of radiation. $1\,\mathrm{eV} = 1.6\cdot10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$. $A = \varepsilon\cdot d\cdot c$ ($d$ is the optical path length, $c$ is the concentration of the absorbing species).

problems.title: [Quantum tunnelling in low-temperature reactions]
problems.problem:
Problem 12 (Physical Chemistry section, problem 3). [Quantum tunnelling in low-temperature reactions]

«I will never be as cold now as I will in the future. The future of cold is infinite. The future of heat is the future of cold». From the movie «Proof». Dedicated to the dear city N.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2018-2-12-fig1.png

At extremely low temperatures (4–100 K), the reaction rate constants can’t be no more described by the Arrhenius law, and the quantum tunnel effect – transition under the potential barrier – becomes the dominant mechanism of the reactions. For the manifestation of the wave properties of particles with mass and velocity $v$, it is necessary for the de Broglie wavelength $\lambda = h/mv$ to exceed the width $d$ of the potential barrier. In addition, classical transitions through the barrier are slow when the barrier height $E$ is greater than $k_\mathrm{B}T$. According to Gol'danskii, tunnel effect dominates under the condition $\lambda/d > k_\mathrm{B}T/E$

The temperature $T_\mathrm{K}$, below which the quantum description of chemical processes becomes necessary, is called the low temperature limit of the reactions.

1. Arrange the particles $\ce{e-}$, C, D, H, Cl in the order of increasing the probability of tunneling. Assume that all particles have the same kinetic energy.

2. Obtain an expression for the temperature $T_\mathrm{K}$ through the parameters $m$, $d$ and $E$, assuming the kinetic energy of the tunneling particle to be $E$.

Tunneling can be exposed not only to electrons and protons, but also heavy atoms and even entire molecules. An example is the reaction of low temperature polymerization of formaldehyde: $\mathrm{H(OCH_2)}_n + \mathrm{OCH_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{H(OCH_2)}_n\mathrm{OCH_2}$.

Knowing that $d_0 = 0.320\,\mathrm{nm}$, $E = 0.1\,\mathrm{eV}$ and taking into account the distance $d_\mathrm{f} = 0.0155\,\mathrm{nm}$ between the adjacent carbon atoms in the final polymer chain, calculate the low temperature limit ($T_\mathrm{K}$) of the formaldehyde polymerization reaction.

At $T_1 = 80\,\mathrm{K}$ average time of linkage to the polymer chain $\tau_{01} = 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{s}$, at lower temperatures it reaches a stationary value $\tau_{02} = 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}$.

4. Determine $\tau_{02}$ for the case of absence of tunneling and the validity of the Arrhenius law. Accept $T_2 = 10\,\mathrm{K}$ and the activation energy of the polymerization reaction to be 8.4 kJ/mol.

Tunneling is a conformationally specific process. An example – the reaction of trifluoromethylhydroxycarbene conversion formed during vacuum pyrolysis of 3,3,3-trifluoro-2-oxopropanoic acid to trifluoroacetaldehyde at 100 K (reactions $\mathbf{2}$ and $\mathbf{3}$). This carbene can be isomerized upon irradiation with wavelength of 465 nm (reaction $\mathbf{1}$). The energies of the ground state of the two isomers have sufficiently close values differing by 3.34 kJ/mol only.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \text{№} & \text{reaction} & d,\ \mathrm{nm} & \Delta H^{\neq},\ \mathrm{eV} \\ \hline \mathbf{1} & \mathbf{A}\leftrightarrow\mathbf{B} & ? & 1.14 \\ \hline \mathbf{2} & \mathbf{A}\rightarrow\mathbf{C} & 0.13 & ? \\ \hline \mathbf{3} & \mathbf{B}\rightarrow\mathbf{C} & 0.20 & 1.18 \end{array}$$

The O–H bond length is of 0.096 nm.

5. Determine for which reactions ($\mathbf{1}$, $\mathbf{2}$ or $\mathbf{3}$) the transport of the hydrogen atom can occur via the tunnel mechanism. Fill the blanks in the table. Assume that the O–H bond position in the cis- and trans- isomers differs by an angle of $111^\circ$. According to the classical theory of transition state, the rate constant $k = \dfrac{k_\mathrm{B}T}{h}\exp\left(-\Delta G^{\neq}/RT\right)$, where $\Delta G^{\neq}$ – Gibbs energy of the transition state. For reaction $\mathbf{2}$: $\Delta S^{\neq} = 856\,\mathrm{J/mol\cdot K}$, $\tau_{1/2} = 72$ days.

problems.title: [A rare transition metal A and its chloride clusters]
problems.problem:
Problem 13 (Inorganic Chemistry section, problem 1). [A rare transition metal A and its chloride clusters]

The silver-white $\mathbf{A}$ transition metal reacts with an excess of 30% hydrogen peroxide forming a solution of $\mathbf{B}$ substance. The solution of $\mathbf{B}$ absorbs ammonia easily forming $\mathbf{C}$ compound. In industry $\mathbf{A}$ is produced from $\mathbf{C}$ substance by hydrogen reduction at $1000\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. $\mathbf{A}$ metal refers to rare and trace elements, it is used mainly as a catalyst and a component of heat resistant and refractory alloys.

$\mathbf{C}$ refers to the compounds where $\mathbf{A}$ presents at the highest oxidation state, but exhibits oxidizing properties only in acidic medium. Thus, the interaction with ammonium iodide in a hydrochloric acid solution leads to the $\mathbf{C}$ reduction with forming of $\mathbf{D}$ and the appearance of a complex color of the solution obtained by mixing of green and brown colors. Melting of $\mathbf{D}$ substance with potassium hydroxide leads to the gas evolution with a sharp odor and $\mathbf{E}$ formation, which reacts with liquid $\ce{SOCl2}$ forming $\mathbf{F}$ stable chloride complex, the solution of which is green. By the reaction between $\mathbf{F}$ solution, ammonia and an oxidizing agent, for example hydrogen peroxide, it is easily to obtain $\mathbf{C}$ once again.

$\mathbf{A}$ forms the range of chlorides, many of them are clusters with different multiplicity of metal-metal bonds. Thus, chlorination of $\mathbf{A}$ at $400\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ leads to the formation of red-brown crystals of $\mathbf{G}$ substance. The structure of $\mathbf{G}$ consists of $\mathrm{Cl_4A(\mu\text{-}Cl)_2ACl_4}$ dimers, in which two octahedra $[\mathrm{ACl_6}]$ are connected by two bridging chlorine atoms. $\mathbf{F}$ can be obtained by fusion of $\mathbf{G}$ with potassium chloride, and in water $\mathbf{G}$ disproportionates to $\mathbf{B}$ and other precipitate product containing $\mathbf{A}$ in its composition. Heating up to ~$150\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ leads to the beginning of $\mathbf{G}$ sublimation, accompanied by decomposition with the formation of chlorine and $\mathbf{H}$ dark red crystals. $\mathbf{H}$ is a diamagnetic substance, what is explained by the presence of multiple metal-metal bonds, and the distance of such bond is less than the one in a simple compound. The interaction of $\mathbf{H}$ with a potassium chloride solution in a concentrated hydrochloric acid gives red crystals of $\mathbf{I}$ compound, which contains $\mathbf{A}$, potassium ($\omega = 10.65\%$) and chlorine ($\omega = 38.63\%$), and the molar mass of $\mathbf{I}$ is 1101.33 g/mol.

1. Determine $\mathbf{A}$ – $\mathbf{I}$ substances. Write down all the mentioned chemical reactions, according to the given scheme. In the $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{G}$, {$\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{D}$}, $\mathbf{H}$ range the oxidation state of $\mathbf{A}$ metal decreases.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2018-2-13-fig1.png

2. Figure the fragments of the crystal structure of $\mathbf{H}$ compound and $\mathbf{I}$ anion part, if it is known that in both compounds there are a threefold axis and a mirror plane perpendicular to it. In addition, in both compounds there are two types of chlorine atoms, with their ratio in $\mathbf{H}$ – 2:1, and in $\mathbf{I}$ – 3:1.

3. The polymerization isomer of $\mathbf{I}$ compound of blue color with a molar mass of 734.22 g/mol is known. Determine the composition of this isomer and depict the structure of its symmetrical diamagnetic anionic part.

The complex $\mathbf{A}$, one of the first stable in air metal complexes of $\mathbf{Me}$ (I) with ligand $\mathbf{X}_\mathbf{n}\mathrm{H}_{\mathbf{n}+3}^{-}$, was synthesized in the mid-1970s by N. Greenwood’s group. In the structure $\mathbf{X}_\mathbf{n}\mathrm{H}_{\mathbf{n}+4}$: the $\mathbf{X}$ atoms are located in the vertices of a pyramid; the number of the skeleton bonds is $\mathbf{n}$ + 2 or $\mathbf{s}$ + $\mathbf{t}$ + $\mathbf{y}$ ($\mathbf{s}$ – number of the bonds $\mathbf{X}$---H---$\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{t}$ – number of the three-center bonds [drawn in the figure below], $\mathbf{y}$ – number of bonds $\mathbf{X}$–$\mathbf{X}$); each $\mathbf{X}$ gives 4 bonds; $\mathbf{X}$ in the vertex of a pyramid is bonded to all the $\mathbf{X}$ atoms in the base with the two- ($\mathbf{XX}$) and the three-center ($\mathbf{XXX}$) bonds; electron density on H in $\mathbf{X}$H$\mathbf{X}$ is higher than in $\mathbf{X}$H.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2018-2-14-fig1.png

3. Calculate $\mathbf{s}$, $\mathbf{t}$, and $\mathbf{y}$ ($\mathbf{y}$ > $\mathbf{t}$) and represent the structural formulae $\mathbf{X}_\mathbf{n}\mathrm{H}_{\mathbf{n}+4}$ and $\mathbf{X}_\mathbf{n}\mathrm{H}_{\mathbf{n}+3}^{-}$.

The compound $\mathbf{B}$, which contains $\mathbf{Me}$ (I) (Vaska’s complex), was obtained by the reaction of $\ce{P(C6H5)3}$, hereinafter $\ce{PPh3}$, with $\mathbf{MeCl_3}$ (64.3 wt.% of $\mathbf{Me}$) in methoxyethanol as solvent, CO source and reductant.

5. Decode the Vaska’s complex formula ($\mathbf{B}$) (67.2 wt.% of $\ce{PPh3}$; 3.57 wt.% of CO) and represent its structural formula, if it is a trans-isomer containing $\ce{Cl-}$.

To obtain $\mathbf{A}$, 0.390 g of $\mathbf{B}$ were dissolved in 20 mL of $\ce{CH2Cl2}$, and all the obtained solution of $\mathrm{K}[\mathbf{X}_\mathbf{n}\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{n}+3}]$ in THF was added at $-70\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, the mixture was heated to $-20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, stirred for 3 hours until changing of color from red to yellow, and forming of KCl and 0.0720 g of $\mathbf{A}$. With the $\mathbf{A}$ formation, the number of atoms in the base of a pyramid $\mathbf{X}_\mathbf{n}\mathrm{H}_{\mathbf{n}+3}^{-}$ increased due to cleavage of the $\mathbf{X}$H$\mathbf{X}$ bond and formation of the $\mathbf{X}$H$\mathbf{Me}$ and $\mathbf{Me}\mathbf{X}$ bonds, and the three-center $\mathbf{X}$H$\mathbf{X}$ remain at different $\mathbf{X}$.

Problem 15 (Inorganic Chemistry section, problem 3). [Peroxy compounds and oxide bronzes]

Some transition metals are formed coordination complexes in which the role of the ligand is performed by $\ce{O2^{2-}}$ peroxide ion. These are the so-called peroxy-compounds. To obtain many of which is possible by simple reaction with hydrogen peroxide.

Thus, when hydrogen peroxide is added to $\mathbf{A}$, freshly precipitated metal oxide of pale orange color ($\omega(\mathrm{O}) = 43.99\%$), an intense red color is observed in the sulfuric medium resulting from the formation of $\mathbf{B}$ complex in which the metal ion coordinates one peroxide ion and the charge of the complex particle is +1. When oxalic acid reacts with a solution obtained by $\mathbf{A}$ and potassium hydroxide dissolving in 3% hydrogen peroxide, an orange color, caused by $\mathbf{E}$ compound, in which the complex anion contains two ion peroxide, is appeared.

In strongly acidic media the reduction of $\mathbf{B}$ to $\mathbf{C}$ occurs. The same process occurs when adding $\mathbf{D}$ oxidizing agent to the $\mathbf{B}$ solution only in the presence of $\ce{Ag+}$ silver ions.

$\mathbf{D}$ is a popular substance as an oxidizer in the analytical practice, as a pesticide, food additive, bleach, a component of explosive mixtures, etc. in industry, $\mathbf{D}$ is a potassium salt of $\mathbf{F}$ acid. $\mathbf{D}$ is obtained by electrolysis of $\mathbf{G}$, acid salt of potassium solution. In this process, the formation of $\mathbf{F}$ acid at the anode occurs, which is neutralized by potassium hydroxide formed in the cathode area. Due to its poor solubility, $\mathbf{D}$ precipitates.

The dissolution of $\mathbf{D}$ in concentrated sulfuric acid upon cooling leads to the formation of $\mathbf{F}$ acid, which decomposes to the other $\mathbf{H}$ acid in the diluted solution upon cooling. This $\mathbf{H}$ acid is very unstable in water, explosive in the crystalline state, it is obtained in two stages. Firstly, $\mathbf{I}$, nonmetal oxide ($\omega(\mathrm{O}) = 59.95\%$), reacts with hydrogen chloride forming $\mathbf{K}$ compound, which further reacts with anhydrous hydrogen peroxide forming $\mathbf{H}$.

1. Determine all unknown substances and write the mentioned equations of chemical reactions according to the given scheme, confirm the data by calculations.

4. $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{H}$ acids belong to a special class of acids. Figure the structure of the anions of these acids and circle the functional group that determines their specificity.

When alloying $\mathbf{A}$ with alkali metal oxides, oxide bronzes are formed. In this process oxygen is lost, and the obtained phases are blue-black colored and possess an electronic conductivity. Depending on the number of embedded atoms, various structural types of bronzes are realized, as shown in the figure (the metal-oxygen framework is shown by polyhedrons, alkali metal atoms are shown in black, the relative amount of alkali metal increases in the α-β-γ bronze range). The simplest α-type is a solid solution with the introduced alkali metal atoms into the metal-oxygen framework of the starting oxide $\mathbf{A}$.

problems.title: [Element X: from the oxalate to the subchlorides]
problems.problem:
Problem 1. [Element X: from the oxalate to the subchlorides]

2019 is the year of the 150th anniversary of the discovery the Periodic Law by the great Russian scientist D.I. Mendeleev. Dmitri Menedeleev’s genius consists not only in the systematization of all the elements known by that time, but also in the prediction of new elements and their properties. Thus, in 1879, the Swedish chemist Lars Nilson discover a new element $\mathbf{X}$, which is a light silver metal with a characteristic yellowish tinge and related to rare and trace elements. The discovery of $\mathbf{X}$ along with other new elements described by Mendeleev became the triumph of the Periodic Law, showed its predictive power and led to the worldwide recognition of this fundamental law of the universe.

Obtaining of $\mathbf{X}$ is a very difficult task, as it requires enrichment and purification through multiple procedures of extraction and precipitation. In the end, sodium oxalate is added to the enriched solution of $\mathbf{X}$ chloride, resulting in the formation of an insoluble substance $\mathbf{A}$. During the thermal decomposition of $\mathbf{A}$ under the temperature less than $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ on air with formation of $\mathbf{B}$ the mass loss is ~ 20%. Upon further heating above $400\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, a white water-insoluble substance $\mathbf{C}$ is formed. The reaction of product $\mathbf{C}$ with sodium fluoride in concentrated hydrochloric acid solution resulting in precipitation of $\mathbf{D}$, that produces chemically pure metal $\mathbf{X}$ under the calcium thermic reaction. Worth noting that complex compound $\mathbf{E}$ is formed due to an excess of sodium fluoride that used for precipitation of $\mathbf{D}$ in industry. Molecular weight of $\mathbf{E}$ 2.235 times higher than that of $\mathbf{D}$.

1. Determine all unknown compound and write the equations of the reactions according to the scheme:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2019-1-1-fig1.png

Metal $\mathbf{X}$ can form clusters in subhalogenide phases, especially with chlorine, which have become known due to work under supervision of the eminent American scientist J. Corbett. In the $\mathbf{F}$, $\mathbf{G}$, $\mathbf{H}$, $\mathbf{I}$ range of subchlorides, the mass fraction of $\mathbf{X}$ increases. $\mathbf{F}$ was synthesized by fusing higher $\mathbf{X}$ metal chloride with powdered $\mathbf{X}$ in a molar ratio of 4:3, respectively, in tantalum crucibles placed in evacuated and sealed quartz ampoules. Prolonged heating of $\mathbf{F}$ leads to its decomposition and the formation of $\mathbf{I}$, the mass loss in this process is 23.95%. The fusion of $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{H}$ is a reaction of coproportionation with the formation of $\mathbf{G}$, during this reaction the oxidation state of $\mathbf{X}$ changes from $\mathbf{F}$ to $\mathbf{G}$ by $\frac{20}{3}\%$ and changes from $\mathbf{H}$ to $\mathbf{G}$ by 12%. The number of metal atoms in the formula unit of $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{H}$ is the same.

2. Calculate the composition of all subchlorides $\mathbf{F}$ – $\mathbf{I}$ and write the mentioned chemical reaction equations.

Problem 2. [Binary compounds A1–A3 and the salts D1, D2]

The mole fraction of element $\mathbf{X}$ in binary compounds $\mathbf{A1}$, $\mathbf{A2}$ and $\mathbf{A3}$ is 25%, and in compound $\mathbf{A2}$ it is nearly equal to mass fraction. At $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ they are solids with ionic crystal structure which decompose at moderate heating. Moreover, at least one simple substance is necessarily present among the decomposition products of each compound. The substance $\mathbf{A3}$ with $\mathbf{X}$ substituted by its lightest analog in the group has a peculiar “mirror twin” $\mathbf{B3}$ (molar fraction of analog of $\mathbf{X}$ equals 75%). The substance $\mathbf{A1}$ can be obtained by the acting of simple substance $\mathbf{Y}$ (gaseous at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) on hydroxide formed by $\mathbf{X}$ at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. In this way 1.207 g $\mathbf{A1}$ can be obtained from 1.000 g of hydroxide.

The substances $\mathbf{D1}$ and $\mathbf{D2}$ being in crystalline state contain the same anion as $\mathbf{A1}$, but they possess rather less stability than $\mathbf{A1}$. The substance $\mathbf{D1}$ decompose totally for 48 hours at ambient temperature, and $\mathbf{D2}$ can exist only at temperatures below $-100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Mass fractions of carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen in $\mathbf{D1}$ are equal to 39.33%, 9.90% and 11.47%, respectively, and $\mathbf{D2}$ does not contain carbon. A portion of $\mathbf{D2}$ decompose totally at temperatures above $-100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, furthermore one of the decomposition products is ionic solid, which can be melt at careful heating (at temperatures above $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) without decomposition, its mass is 1.65 times less than the mass of initial portion.

Problem 3. [Cathode and anode materials of lithium-ion batteries]

A cathode of modern lithium-ion batteries contains redox-active lithium salt (for example, lithium iron phosphate) as the active component. This compound can be prepared via heating of an aqueous solution of stoichiometric mixture of $\ce{LiOH}$, $\ce{H3PO4}$, and $\ce{FeSO4}$ at pH 7–8 ($\ce{LiFePO4}$ is the least soluble and is therefore the only reaction product under the said conditions).

Calculate the total mass of lithium-ion battery (cathode – $\ce{LiNi_{1/3}Co_{1/3}Mn_{1/3}O2}$, anode – graphite, mass of other components is 20% of the battery mass) which has the capacity sufficient for charging three times a typical smartphone (its battery capacity is $3500\,\mathrm{mA{\cdot}h}$). Problem 4. [Rate-determining steps]

In chemical kinetics a notion “rate-determining step” is often used in study of reaction mechanisms. This notion relates to the approximation in experimental kinetic curves analysis. It is assumed that specific part of the curve or maybe the whole curve corresponds to the particular kinetic step which determines the rate of the complex process under consideration in given moment of time. It was found that in consecutive reactions the slowest step is rate-determining while in parallel reactions the fastest one.

For the following scheme of obtaining of the substance $\mathbf{Z}$ (all steps are elementary and take place in solution) find the rate-determining step and prove it via calculation of instantaneous rates, where possible. Problem 5. [Linear compounds A–E: combustion analysis]

Linear unbranched substances $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$, and $\mathbf{E}$ form an extremely important family of biologically active compounds involved in regulation of various bioprocesses, mostly in cell nucleus.

The 1.00 g weighed amounts of $\mathbf{B}$ – $\mathbf{E}$ were burned in an excess of oxygen. The masses ($m$) of carbon dioxide formed and the volumes ($V$) of the gas $\mathbf{X}$ left unabsorbed after bubbling the combustion products through an alkali solution are given in the hereunder table. Besides, the numbers of atom types of an element found in $\mathbf{X}$ and hydrogen for each of $\mathbf{B}$ – $\mathbf{E}$ are given there.

problems.title: [Back titration of carbon dioxide absorbed by ammonia]
problems.problem:
Problem 8. [Back titration of carbon dioxide absorbed by ammonia]

Reverse titration is a technique often used in titrimetry. It involves introducing an excess of titrant and titrating the unreacted titrant upon the completion of the reaction. This technique was used to determine the concentration of $\ce{CO2}$ absorbed from the air by an excess of ammonia solution. With that purpose, $5.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of the resulting solution were mixed with $20\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $\ce{BaCl2}$ solution (5 wt.%), $10.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $0.5000\,\mathrm{M}$ NaOH solution, an indicator and an excess of formaldehyde forming hexamethylene tetramine $\ce{(CH2)6N4}$ with ammonia. The obtained solution was titrated with $0.5000\,\mathrm{M}$ solution HCl, which required $V_1$ mL of the acid.

1. Write down the equations: a) of the reaction occurring during $\ce{CO2}$ binding with the $\ce{NH3}$ solution; formaldehyde reactions: b) with ammonia; c) with the resulting ammonium salt.

2. What form of $\ce{CO2}$ prevails in an aqueous solution at pH 8.0? Justify the answer. The acidity constants of carbonic acid: $K_1 = 4.3\cdot10^{-7}$, $K_2 = 4.7\cdot10^{-11}$.

3. a) What is the added alkali spent for? Write down the reaction equation. What is the role of the added barium salt? Write in ionic form the equation of the barium ion reaction. What is HCl spent for when titrating in the presence of $\ce{BaCl2}$ and using phenolphthalein as indicator (color transition occurs at pH ~ 8)? Write down the reaction (note that HCl does not dissolve the precipitate during the titration).

b) What would HCl be consumed for during the described determination of $\ce{CO2}$ if the barium salt would not have been added to the mixture? Write down the equations of these reactions.

4. a) Calculate the $\ce{CO2}$ content (mol/L) in the ammonia solution being analyzed, if the hydrochloric acid volume $V_1$ spent for titration equals $9.80\,\mathrm{mL}$.

b) What volume of HCl would be spent for the titration without the barium salt?

5. An ammonia solution titrated according to this protocol, containing some excess of HCl and having a pH of 4.0, was decanted and left in the laboratory in a stoppered vessel. After 1 month, the pH of the mixture became equal to 4.4.

problems.title: [Moseley's law and X-ray spectra]
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (Physical Chemistry section, problem 1). [Moseley's law and X-ray spectra]

«Periodic law is not threatened with destruction but only superstructures and development are promises …» D.I. Mendeleev

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2019-2-1-fig1.png

Figure 1. X-ray spectra

2019 was announced as The International Year of the Periodic Table of Chemical Elements and is dedicated to its 150th anniversary. The periodicity of properties is determined by the charge ($Z$) of the atomic nuclei, which was experimentally determined by Henry Moseley in the study of the X-ray spectra of chemical elements. He found that an atom of each chemical element emits X-rays of strictly defined energies. When an electron gets sufficient energy an electron is removed from the inner shell and the atom transitions to an excited state. To return to the ground state, the electron from a further shell must go to the released one. In this case, the excess energy is released in the form of X-rays. The transition from the L-shell to K causes $\mathrm{K_\alpha}$-radiation, the transition M → K gives $\mathrm{K_\beta}$-radiation.

The wavelength of X-rays emitted during a transition from the energy level $m$ to $n$ is defined as

$$\frac{1}{\lambda} = R(Z-\sigma)^2\left(\frac{1}{n^2}-\frac{1}{m^2}\right),$$

where $R$ – Rydberg constant, $\sigma$ – screening constant, $(Z-\sigma)$ – effective nuclear charge. In general case, the Moseley law can be written as $1/\lambda = C(Z-\sigma)^2$.

1. Determine the constant $C$ (in $R$ units) for $\mathrm{K_\alpha}$- and $\mathrm{K_\beta}$-radiation.

2. Figure 1 shows a typical view of the X-ray spectrum. Match peaks 1 and 2 with $\mathrm{K_\alpha}$- and $\mathrm{K_\beta}$-radiation.

Figure 2 shows the dependence of $E^{1/2}$ of X-ray $\mathrm{K_\alpha}$-radiation on the atomic number of chemical elements. By the dependence linearization, the equation is obtained $y = a + bx$, where $a = -3.74$; $b = 3.22$.

3. Based on these data and expressions for the Moseley law calculate: a) the screening constant $\sigma$; b) Rydberg constant ($\mathrm{m^{-1}}$).

4. Determine the element $\mathbf{A}$. If you didn’t manage to determine $\sigma$ and $R$ from previous question, accept $R = 3.29\cdot10^{15}\,\mathrm{Hz}$, $\sigma = 1$.

Figure 2. Dependence of X-ray energy on the nuclear charge of elements

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2019-2-1-fig2.png

The main sources of X-ray radiation are X-ray tubes and radioisotopes. The voltage ($U$) between the electrodes of the tube determines the minimum wavelength of bremsstrahlung radiation.

5. Determine the voltage (kV) between the electrodes of the X-ray tube that was applied when recording the X-ray spectrum shown in Figure 1. Assume that all the energy $eU$ ($e$ – electron charge) imparted to the electron flux is spent on the generation of X-ray radiation with the energy $h\nu_\mathrm{max}$.

6. a) Calculate the energy that must be given to an atom of the last element ($Z = 30$) from the series shown in Figure 2 for removing an electron from the inner shell.

b) Which of the radioisotopes listed in the table can be used to record the spectra of a number of elements from Figure 2?

$$\begin{array}{c|c} \text{Radioisotope} & \text{Energy emitted in a nuclear reaction, keV} \\ \hline ^{26}\mathrm{Al} & 1809 \text{ and } 511 \\ \hline ^{56}\mathrm{Co} & 122 \text{ and } 14 \\ \hline ^{241}\mathrm{Am} & 59.2 \end{array}$$

c) For $^{26}$Al and $^{56}$Co two values of energy are given, since their nuclei can undergo both $\beta^+$ decay and electron capture. Write the equations for the corresponding reactions for $^{26}$Al.

7. Give an example of the sequence of arrangement of elements in the periodic table, which didn’t agree with the choice of atomic mass as a criterion of the periodicity of chemical properties.

Physical constants: $h = 6.63\cdot10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s}$, $c = 2.998\cdot10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $1\,\mathrm{eV} = 1.6\cdot10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$, $e = 1.6\cdot10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$.

problems.title: [Racemization of a cobalt(III) EDTA complex]
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (Physical Chemistry section, problem 2). [Racemization of a cobalt(III) EDTA complex]

Mellor et al. explained the big difference in the period of the half-life of racemization in the acidic medium of $d$-$\ce{Co(EDTA)^-}$ ($\mathbf{A}$) $\leftrightarrows$ $l$-$\ce{Co(EDTA)^-}$ ($\mathbf{B}$) ($t_{1/2}$ = 2 weeks ($30\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) and 170 minutes ($100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$)) by the formation of the intermediate $\ce{Co[N2(CH2COO)3CH2COO]^-}$ ($\mathbf{A'}$) with the cleavage of the Co–O bond.

1. Calculate $k_\mathrm{obs}$ ($\mathrm{s^{-1}}$) at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and show that in $r = k_\mathrm{obs}\cdot[\mathbf{A}]$, $[\mathbf{A}]$ and $k_\mathrm{obs}$ depend on pH, considering equilibria $\mathbf{A} \leftrightarrows \mathbf{A'}$ ($k_1$; $k_{-1}$); $\mathbf{A'}\mathrm{H} \leftrightarrows \mathbf{A'} + \ce{H+}$ ($K_\mathrm{a}$) and material balance.

In 1962, Busch et al. denied this mechanism, showing that at pH ≤ 2 $k_\mathrm{obs}$ does not depend on $[\ce{H+}]$ and equals to $4.018\cdot10^{-6}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ ($100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$); $3.110\cdot10^{-10}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ ($45\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$). They explained this by trigonal twisting in the intramolecular mechanism (Bailar) $\mathbf{A} \leftrightarrows \mathbf{A'}$ ($k_1$; $k_{-1}$); $\mathbf{A'} \rightarrow \mathbf{B}$ ($k_2$) with the formation of the trigonal prismatic intermediate $\mathbf{A'}$.

2. Calculate $E_\mathrm{a}$ and $\Delta H^{\#}$, $\Delta S^{\#}$, $K^{\#} = k_1/k_{-1}$ at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ for $\mathbf{A} \leftrightarrows \mathbf{A'}$ ($k_1$; $k_{-1}$).

3. Describe the mechanism of $\mathbf{A} \leftrightarrows \mathbf{A'} \rightarrow \mathbf{B}$ with structural formulas, derive the kinetic equation using the method of stationary approximations.

In alkaline medium, the racemization rate is much higher and depends on the pH. Thus, at $45\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $C_\mathbf{A} = 0.01\,\mathrm{mol/L}$, the rate is described by a second-order reaction equation, which is possible in the case of the mechanism: $\mathbf{A} + \ce{OH^-} \leftrightarrows \mathbf{A'}\ce{OH^-}$ ($k_3$; $k_{-3}$), $\mathbf{A'}\ce{OH^-} \rightarrow \mathbf{B}$ ($k_4$) with the formation of monocapped trigonal prism $\mathbf{A'}\ce{OH^-}$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} \text{pH} & 10.30 & 11.50 & 12.26 & 13.02 \\ \hline r,\ \mathrm{mol/L{\cdot}s} & 1.08\cdot10^{-6} & 1.71\cdot10^{-5} & 9.83\cdot10^{-5} & 5.65\cdot10^{-4} \end{array}$$

4. Derive the kinetic equation of racemization using the method of stationary approximations, and calculate $k_\mathrm{obs}$ ($\mathrm{L/mol{\cdot}s}$).

5. According to the derived equation, calculate the racemization rate at pH = 5 ($\mathrm{mol/L{\cdot}s}$) and compare it with the experimental $8.50\cdot10^{-10}\,\mathrm{mol/L{\cdot}s}$.

As a result, Busch et al came to the conclusion that, at any pH, racemization is described by a two-step mechanism, in which each stage includes two elementary stages, the intermediate is a monocapped trigonal prism, and $k_\mathrm{obs} = k + k' C_{\ce{OH^-}}$

6. Suggest a mechanism common to any pH, derive the kinetic equation.

7. By calculation using this equation, show that the calculated rate for $45\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and the experimental one at pH = 5 coincide.

For reference: $\ln\frac{C^0}{C} = kt$; $k = A\mathrm{e}^{-E_\mathrm{a}/RT}$; $\ln\frac{k_2}{k_1} = \frac{E_\mathrm{a}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1}-\frac{1}{T_2}\right)$; $E_\mathrm{a} - \Delta H^{\#} = nRT$; $\Delta S^{\#} = R\left(\ln A - \ln T - \ln\frac{k_\mathrm{B}}{h} - n\right)$, where $n$ – molecularity of the reaction; $t$ – time; $k_\mathrm{B} = 1.381\cdot10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J/K}$; $h = 6.626\cdot10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J{\cdot}s}$.

problems.title: [Heating a country house with propane]
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (Physical Chemistry section, problem 3). [Heating a country house with propane]

A common fuel for winter heating of country houses in Russia is liquefied bottled gas, usually a mixture of propane and butane.

The owner came home in winter and found that the temperature in the room and outside was $-10\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and lit the burner. The liquid propane balloon is outside. The barometer on the wall showed that the atmospheric pressure was 760 mm Hg. The size of the heated room is $20\,\mathrm{m^2}\times2.5\,\mathrm{m}$.

What is the maximum (theoretically possible, without reducer) intensity $I$ of the supply (g/s) of propane when the gas enters the combustion site through a wide pipe, and the molecules that have left the balloon do not return to it. problems.title: [Transaminases and the King–Altman method]
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (Life Sciences and Polymers section, problem 2). [Transaminases and the King–Altman method]

Enzymatic reactions involving reversible transfer of an amino group from a donor to an acceptor play the key role in integration of nitrogen and energy metabolism in organisms. Thus, as a result of a transamination reaction, a canonical α-amino acid $\mathbf{A}$ transforms into α-keto acid $\mathbf{B}$ (54.54% O by mass), whereas α-keto acid $\mathbf{C}$ (41.09% C by mass) into canonical α-amino acid $\mathbf{D}$ bearing total negative charge at pH 7. The amino group transfer does not lead to a change of the number of carbon atoms in the donor molecule.

1. Draw structures of $\mathbf{A}$ – $\mathbf{D}$.

Transamination reactions catalyzed by enzymes referred to as transaminases usually follow the so-called “ping-pong” mechanism, which can be described by the hereunder kinetic scheme:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2019-2-5-fig1.png

E and E' represent the enzyme in its initial and intermediate states, respectively; $\mathrm{S_1}$ and $\mathrm{S_2}$ are substrates; and $\mathrm{P_1}$ and $\mathrm{P_2}$ are the reaction products.

Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) is the co-factor of transaminases in their initial state. PLP is firmly bound to the protein active site via phosphate group and nitrogen atom making involvement of the latter in the catalysis impossible. It is the amino group of the substrate that interacts with PLP.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2019-2-5-fig2.png

2. Choose the roles (enzyme, amino group acceptor, amino group donor, enzyme-substrate complex) specific to particles $\mathrm{ES_1}$, $\mathrm{ES_2}$, $\mathrm{S_1}$, and $\mathrm{S_2}$ (scheme (1)).

3. Based on the PLP structure, draw the cofactor forms found in particles $\mathrm{ES_1}$, E', and $\mathrm{E'S_2}$ (scheme (1)).

Kinetics of complicated enzymatic reactions can be described using the King-Altman method based on the graph theory. Let us consider the approach using the two-step Michaelis-Menten scheme as an example:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2019-2-5-fig3.png

a) First one has to draw a directed graph with the vertices corresponding to all the enzyme forms and the directed edges (arrows) reflecting all possible enzyme transformations. An expression of the reaction rate is attributed to each edge; all such expressions do not include the enzyme in any of its forms (E and ES are not written in the example under consideration).

b) ES transformation into E occurs via two parallel routs: as a result of dissociation ($k_{-1}$) and the product formation ($k_2$). Parallel transformations are summed up ($k_{-1}+k_2$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2019-2-5-fig4.png

c) Next, one needs to find spanning trees for each vertex of the constructed graph. A tree is defined as a fragment of the initial graph containing all its vertices and a subset of loop-free edges, which allows reaching the target vertex starting from any other one. There is only one spanning tree for each vertex in scheme (2):

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2019-2-5-fig5.png

d) For each spanning tree, expressions attributed to its edges are multiplied giving the product. If a vertex has several spanning trees, the obtained products are summed up. The finally obtained expression referred to as determinant is denoted as w(En), where En is the vertex under consideration. Thus, for scheme (2) $w(\mathrm{E}) = k_{-1}+k_2$, $w(\mathrm{ES}) = k_1[\mathrm{S}]$.

e) The expression of the reaction rate is given as the determinant of the enzyme form leading to the reaction product multiplied by the rate constant of the step leading to the reaction product and the initial enzyme concentration, divided by the sum of determinants of all the enzyme forms:

$$v = \frac{k_2k_1[\mathrm{S}][\mathrm{E_0}]}{k_{-1}+k_2+k_1[\mathrm{S}]} = \frac{k_2[\mathrm{S}][\mathrm{E_0}]}{K_M+[\mathrm{S}]} \quad \text{where } K_M = \frac{k_{-1}+k_2}{k_1} \qquad (6)$$

4. Draw the directed graph for the “ping-pong” mechanism.

5. Draw all spanning trees for E, $\mathrm{ES_1}$, E', and $\mathrm{E'S_2}$.

6. Write down the determinants $w(\mathrm{E})$, $w(\mathrm{ES_1})$, $w(\mathrm{E'})$, and $w(\mathrm{E'S_2})$.

7. Write down the expression for the rate of $\mathrm{P_2}$ formation.

problems.problem:
Problem 7 (Inorganic Chemistry section, problem 1). [The compound YNX₃ and its sulfonate derivatives]

The generally accepted laboratory method of obtaining the $\mathbf{Y}\mathrm{N}\mathbf{X}_3$ solution ($w_\mathrm{N} = 42.42\%$) is the multistage reduction of $\ce{HNO2}$ with the $\ce{HSO3^-}$ solution.

1. Decode $\mathbf{Y}\mathrm{N}\mathbf{X}_3$ and write the total equation of its synthesis.

$\mathbf{Y}\mathrm{N}\mathbf{X}_3$ is characterized by the formation of cations ($\mathbf{Z}^+$) in acidified solutions, although a number of sulfonate derivatives with formation of anions are known.

2. Calculate the content (α, mol.%) of cations in 0.01 mol/L aqueous solution of $\mathbf{Y}\mathrm{N}\mathbf{X}_3$ (pH=3, $K_\mathrm{B} = 6.6\cdot10^{-9}$).

Two of the sulfonate derivatives are formed during the synthesis of $\mathbf{Y}\mathrm{N}\mathbf{X}_3$ in very fast stages, which does not allow them to be isolated from solution. Therefore, sulfonate derivatives are obtained in the form of salts from alkaline solutions. At $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and 1 atm, $22.40\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $\ce{SO2}$ and $0.08500\,\mathrm{g}$ of $\ce{KNO2}$ are dissolved in $100\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $0.01\,\mathrm{mol/L}$ KOH solution, and then another $22.40\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $\ce{SO2}$ are passed through to form $0.1292\,\mathrm{g}$ of salt $\mathbf{A}$ (48% yield). Careful hydrolysis of $\mathbf{A}$ gives salt $\mathbf{B}$, which has one N–S bond less than in $\mathbf{A}$.

3. Establish two possible anions $\mathbf{1}$ and $\mathbf{2}$ that could be formed in the solution, if their M differ by 1 g/mol, and $\mathbf{2}$ has no $\mathbf{Y}$ – $\mathbf{X}$ bond. Decode $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$.

4. Give a complete scheme for the synthesis of $\mathbf{Y}\mathrm{N}\mathbf{X}_3$, if after the formation of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ the solution is treated with HCl ($100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) until the salt with cation $\mathbf{Z}^+$ is formed, further treatment of its suspension with NaOBu in butanol gives a precipitate of NaCl and a solution of $\mathbf{Y}\mathrm{N}\mathbf{X}_3$.

Rubidium salt $\mathbf{E}$, which anion does not contain $\mathbf{X}$ and the bond distances are nearly the same as in $\mathbf{A}$, was isolated from the strong alkali solution of $\mathbf{A}$. The salt $\mathbf{I}$ was obtained from the solution of $\mathbf{A}$, bearing the anions $\mathbf{1}$ and $\mathbf{2}$ at pH~12. The anion of salt $\mathbf{I}$ has twice as many N–S bonds in comparison with $\mathbf{E}$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{Salt} & \text{N, wt.\%} & \text{S, wt.\%} & \mathbf{X}\text{, wt.\%} & \text{Rb, wt.\%} & \text{N–}\mathbf{Y}\text{, nm} & \text{S–}\mathbf{Y}\text{, nm} & \mathbf{Y}\text{–}\mathbf{X}\text{–}\mathbf{Y}\text{, nm} & \text{N–S, nm} \\ \hline \mathbf{E} & 2.80 & 12.79 & 1.20 & & 0.143 & 0.145 & — & 0.175 \\ \hline \mathbf{I} & 3.25 & & 0.81 & 49.57 & 0.142 & 0.144 & 0.241 & 0.172 \end{array}$$

5. Decode $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{I}$.

6. Draw the structural formulas of anions of salts $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{I}$.

Problem 8 (Inorganic Chemistry section, problem 2). [Compounds A1–A5 and C1–C3 of the same qualitative composition]

Compounds in the groups $\mathbf{A1}$ – $\mathbf{A3}$ and $\mathbf{C1}$ – $\mathbf{C3}$ have the same qualitative composition but differ in the quantitative composition; the mass fraction of oxygen is decreased over the $\mathbf{A1}$ – $\mathbf{A3}$ and $\mathbf{C1}$ – $\mathbf{C3}$ series. Pale-yellow liquid $\mathbf{A1}$ is the only product of interaction between oxides $\mathbf{B}$ (43.98 wt.% O) and $\mathbf{C1}$ (74.06 wt.% O) taken in the 1:3 molar ratio (reaction 1). The treatment of oxide $\mathbf{B}$ with a mixture of oxalic and dilute nitric acids at heating yields blue-green crystals of $\mathbf{A2}$ (reaction 2), but the latter product can be prepared more conveniently via an exchange reaction in a solution (reaction 3). The interaction between elementary compound $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{C2}$ at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in the presence of acetonitrile gives compounds $\mathbf{A3}$ (dark-red crystals) and $\mathbf{C3}$ (reaction 4). Heating of $\mathbf{A3}$ under inert atmosphere gives a mixture of $\mathbf{B}$ and the products of decomposition of $\mathbf{C1}$ (reaction 5). A molecule of $\mathbf{A1}$ has a mirror plane, and the atoms of the elements forming oxides $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C1}$ are not connected in the structure of $\mathbf{A1}$.

1. Determine compounds $\mathbf{A2}$ – $\mathbf{A3}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C1}$ – $\mathbf{C3}$, $\mathbf{D}$. Write the equations of reactions 1 – 5.

2. For compound $\mathbf{A1}$, draw a structure of its molecular form and of its two ionic forms differing in the nature of the central atom of the cation and anion.

3. Determine the coordination polyhedron of the central atom in $\mathbf{A1}$ and its coordination number.

Heating of oxide $\mathbf{B}$ with $\ce{SOCl2}$ gives pale-yellow liquid $\mathbf{E}$ (reaction 6), the treatment of which with HF affords white powder $\mathbf{F}$ (45.98 wt.% F) (reaction 7). The interaction of the latter with $\mathbf{G}$ (a derivative of silane, the only signal in the $^1$H NMR spectrum is a singlet at 0.22 ppm relative to tetramethylsilane, 24.38 wt.% Si) leads to the formation of compound $\mathbf{A4}$, qualitative composition of which is the same as that of $\mathbf{A1}$ – $\mathbf{A3}$ (reaction 8). $\mathbf{A4}$ is dark-red powder, decomposing with explosion upon heating to $120\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

4. Write the equations of reactions 6 – 8, determine compounds $\mathbf{E}$ – $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{A4}$.

Another compound the qualitative composition of which is the same as for compound $\mathbf{A1}$ – $\mathbf{A4}$, can hypothetically be obtained via the scheme drawn below (this synthesis has not been succeeded yet because of extreme instability of $\mathbf{A5}$):

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2019-2-8-fig1.png

problems.title: [Tetrahedrite as a thermoelectric material]
problems.problem:
Problem 9 (Inorganic Chemistry section, problem 3). [Tetrahedrite as a thermoelectric material]

The natural mineral tetrahedrite with composition $\mathrm{Cu_{12}}\mathbf{X}_4\mathrm{S_{13}}$ is currently a highly efficient thermoelectric material. The brown gas and white precipitate $\mathbf{A}$ was formed under the decomposition of tetrahedrite by concentrated nitric acid. The filtered precipitate reacts with zinc in hydrochloric acid solution to form gas $\mathbf{B}$, which, when passed through a heated glass tube, decomposes to form a metal mirror on the inner surface of the tube. This mirror does not dissolve in alkaline sodium hypochlorite solution.

1. Identify unknown compounds and write the mentioned chemical reactions if it is known that the oxidation state of $\mathbf{X}$ element in a tetrahedrite is less than in $\mathbf{A}$.

The mineral crystallizes in a cubic system with a unit cell parameter of 10.33 Å. In single unit cell of a tetrahedrite: twenty-four copper atoms are located on the edges of the unit cell, the same number of copper atoms – on the faces, and the remaining six copper atoms are located inside the unit cell.

2. Calculate the number of formula units in single unit cell of tetrahedrite and indicate the number of sulfur atoms located inside the unit cell, if it is known that all remaining sulfur atoms occupy only the vertices of the unit cell.

3. Calculate the theoretical density of tetrahedrite.

The efficiency of a thermoelectric material is estimated using the dimensionless thermoelectric figure of merit $ZT$, which is calculated as $ZT = S^2\cdot T/(\rho\cdot\kappa)$, where $S$ is the Seebeck coefficient of the material, $T$ is the absolute temperature, $\rho$ is the specific electrical resistance of the material, $\kappa$ is the thermal conductivity of the material. The following values were experimentally obtained for tetrahedrite (see the Table).

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} T,\ \mathrm{K} & S,\ \mathrm{V/K} & \kappa,\ \mathrm{W/m{\cdot}K} & ZT \\ \hline 300 & 2.2\cdot10^{-4} & 0.5 & 0.9075 \\ \hline 600 & 2.5\cdot10^{-4} & 1.5 & 1.25 \end{array}$$

4. Calculate the tetrahedrite band gap $E_\mathrm{g}$, if it is known that it is related to the specific electrical conductivity ($\sigma$) by the Arrhenius equation $\sigma(T) = \sigma_0\cdot\exp(-E_\mathrm{g}/(2k_\mathrm{B}\cdot T))$. The Boltzmann constant is taken equal to $8.617\cdot10^{-5}\,\mathrm{eV/K}$.

The thermoelectric efficiency of tetrahedrite is increased by chemical modification. For example, the substitution of copper atoms by iron leads to a fast increase of the thermoelectric figure of merit.

5. Calculate the composition of iron-substituted tetrahedrite, if it is known that copper in tetrahedrite exists in two oxidation states: +1 and +2. The number of copper atoms in +2 oxidation state has decreased by 2 times, and all iron atoms possess +3 oxidation state after substitution.

problems.title: [σ- and π-aromaticity]
problems.problem:
Problem 10 (Organic Chemistry section, problem 1). [σ- and π-aromaticity]

For most chemists the definition of aromaticity is in the following phrase:

“In order for a molecule to be aromatic, it must contain at least one planar cycle, each of whose atoms has a p-orbital suitable for the formation of an aromatic system. In this cycle there should be 4n+2 (i.e. 2, 6, 10, 14, 18, 22, etc.) electrons”

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2019-2-10-fig1.png

Figure 1 German mark dedicated to the discovery of the benzene molecule

Recently, however, the concept of aromaticity has significantly expanded. It was shown that planar systems formed not only by π- but also by σ-bonds can be aromatic, subject to the Hückel’s rule. So, using the expanded definition of aromaticity the following facts can be easily explain:

A. Cation $\mathbf{A}$ with $m/z = 3$ is found in significant quantities in interstellar space

B. Laser evaporation of a mixture of Al with $\ce{Na2CO3}$ leads to formation of a negatively charged $\mathbf{B}$ ion with $m/z = 131$, which has fourth-order symmetry axis.

C. Crystal structure of compound $\ce{Li12Si7}$ is $(\mathrm{Li_6^{6+}}[\mathbf{C}])_2\,(\mathrm{Li_{12}^{10+}}[\mathrm{Si_4}]^{10-})_2$

D. Crystalline sodium amalgam $\ce{Na3Hg2}$ contains square planar anion $\mathbf{D}$.

E. An anion $\mathbf{E}$ was detected during the study of the bimetallic Pt–Zn system in catalytic hydrogenation, the mass spectrum of $\mathbf{E}$ is presented in Fig. 2. It is also known that $\mathbf{E}$ has 5th order symmetry axis and all hydrogen atoms in it are in the same plane with the platinum atom.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2019-2-10-fig2.png

Figure 2 Mass-spectra of D anion

1. Give the structure of the particles $\mathbf{A}$ – $\mathbf{E}$ and indicate the number of electrons that are involved in the formation of the aromatic system.

In addition to σ-aromatic compounds, chemists managed to obtain molecules, which structures are stabilized with both π-and σ-aromaticity. The history of this type of compounds began in 1988, when it was discovered that oxidation of an orange crystalline binary compound $\mathbf{F}$ (containing 8.65% of element $\mathbf{X}$) in the $\ce{H2O2}$ – $\ce{(CF3SO2)2O}$ – $\ce{CF3SO3H}$ system lead to a blue ionic compound $\mathbf{G}$ (containing 8.49% of element $\mathbf{X}$). The spectral properties of compound $\mathbf{G}$ confirmed its double aromaticity, but it was not possible to investigate its structure in the crystalline state challenged such hypothesis. In the same year, the structure of the purple crystalline ionic compound $\mathbf{N}$ was investigated; however, in this case, it turned out that dication $\mathbf{N}$ was less symmetric than expected. It was possible to unequivocally obtain the compound and prove double aromaticity only in 2018. The synthesis was performed in two stages. In the first stage, the colorless crystalline binary compound $\mathbf{O}$ (containing 13.07% of element $\mathbf{X}$) was treated with an excess of PhSeNa yielding yellow crystals $\mathbf{P}$. Treatment of P with two equivalents of $\ce{NOSbF6}$ led to the formation of green-blue crystals $\mathbf{Q}$ (contains 34.07% of element $\mathbf{X}$). Their study showed that all Se–Se distances in $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{Q}$ are equal, but their values are 3.38 Å and 3.26 Å, respectively.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2019-2-10-fig3.png

Scheme 1. Synthesis of ionic cimpound N.

2. Decode element $\mathbf{X}$ and compounds $\mathbf{F}$ – $\mathbf{Q}$. It is known that compound $\mathbf{I}$ has a third-order symmetry axis, compounds $\mathbf{J}$ and $\mathbf{L}$ have a sixth-order symmetry axis, and cation $\mathbf{N}$ – a second-order symmetry axis.

The molecule of grandisol was first isolated in 1967 and it is one of the pheromones of the cotton weevil (Anthonomus grandis), a large pest of cotton plants. The cotton industry was seriously affected by the weevil invasion in the 1970s. To combat these insects was used a 4-component mixture, in which Grandisol is the main component.
